EA-CH-001.name: Geography of East Asia
EA-CH-001.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-001.description: East Asia encompasses China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia, and Taiwan, shaped by major river systems including the Yellow River and Yangtze that enabled early agricultural civilizations.

EA-CH-002.name: Pan Gu and Nu Wa
EA-CH-002.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-002.description: Chinese creation myth: Pan Gu separated heaven and earth; Nu Wa repaired the sky and created humanity from yellow clay, foundational myths of Chinese cosmology.

EA-CH-003.name: Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa
EA-CH-003.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-003.description: Major cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE) with advanced urban planning, grid streets, drainage systems, and the Great Bath, located in present-day Pakistan.

EA-CH-004.name: Indus Valley Urban Planning
EA-CH-004.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-004.description: Harappan cities featured standardized baked-brick construction, grid-pattern streets, sophisticated drainage and sewage, and uniformity suggesting strong centralized planning authority.

EA-CH-005.name: The Great Bath of Mohenjo-Daro
EA-CH-005.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-005.description: A large brick pool at Mohenjo-Daro, possibly used for ritual bathing, representing one of the earliest known public water facilities and the engineering sophistication of Harappan culture.

EA-CH-006.name: Zhou Dynasty (1046-256 BCE)
EA-CH-006.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-006.description: The Zhou Dynasty ruled China for nearly 800 years, the longest dynastic period. The Mandate of Heaven justified their rule. Eastern Zhou divided into Spring & Autumn (770-476 BCE) and Warring States (475-221 BCE) periods.

EA-CH-007.name: Mandate of Heaven
EA-CH-007.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-007.description: The Zhou concept that heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous dynasty; a lost mandate justified rebellion. This doctrine became central to Chinese political philosophy for millennia.

EA-CH-008.name: Zhou Feudalism
EA-CH-008.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-008.description: The Zhou political system organized land into hierarchical fiefs: king at top, then dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons, each owing military service and tribute to superiors.

EA-CH-009.name: Spring and Autumn Period
EA-CH-009.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-009.description: Period (770-476 BCE) named for the Spring and Autumn Annals, marked by declining Zhou royal power, the rise of regional hegemons, and constant interstate warfare that drove philosophical innovation.

EA-CH-010.name: Warring States Period
EA-CH-010.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-010.description: Period (475-221 BCE) of intensified warfare among seven major states, mass infantry armies, technological innovation including iron weapons, and the flourishing of competing philosophical schools.

EA-CH-011.name: Hundred Schools of Thought
EA-CH-011.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-011.description: Flourishing of philosophical and intellectual traditions during the late Zhou, including Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, Mohism, and others competing for state patronage.

EA-CH-012.name: Confucius (551-479 BCE)
EA-CH-012.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-012.description: Born into a minor noble family, became a minister for the State of Lu. His philosophy emphasized relationships between family and society, with filial piety as the most important principle. Teachings compiled in The Analects.

EA-CH-013.name: The Five Relationships
EA-CH-013.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-013.description: Confucian framework: father/son, elder/younger brother, husband/wife, friend, and ruler/subject. Each relationship carries specific duties and hierarchies, structuring social and political life.

EA-CH-014.name: Filial Piety
EA-CH-014.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-014.description: Central Confucian virtue of respect and care for parents and ancestors, the foundation for all other relationships. Failure in filial duty was considered the root of social disorder.

EA-CH-015.name: The Analects
EA-CH-015.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-015.description: Compilation of Confucius's teachings and dialogues collected by his disciples, the primary source for Confucian philosophy and one of the Four Books of classical Chinese education.

EA-CH-016.name: Daoism and Laozi
EA-CH-016.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-016.description: Daoist philosophy emphasizes living in harmony with the Dao (the Way), spontaneity, and simplicity, in contrast to Confucian social rituals. Laozi is traditionally credited as founder and author of the Daodejing.

EA-CH-017.name: The Daodejing
EA-CH-017.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-017.description: Classical Daoist text attributed to Laozi, presenting the Dao as the source of all existence, advocating wu-wei (non-forcing action), softness over hardness, and humility as paths to harmony.

EA-CH-018.name: Yin and Yang
EA-CH-018.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-018.description: Daoist concept of complementary opposites, where each side contains the seed of the other. Yin represents earth, dark, cold, female; Yang represents heaven, light, hot, male. Their balance produces harmony.

EA-CH-019.name: Legalism and Hanfeizi
EA-CH-019.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-019.description: Legalist philosophy argued that human nature is selfish and that strict laws, harsh punishments, and state control are necessary for order. Hanfeizi synthesized the Legalist doctrines of Shang Yang and Shen Buhai.

EA-CH-020.name: Mohism and Universal Love
EA-CH-020.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-020.description: Mozi founded Mohism, arguing for impartial concern (jian ai) for all people, against Confucian partiality toward kin. Mohists championed defensive warfare, frugality, and merit-based governance.

EA-CH-021.name: Yin Dynasty and Bronze Age
EA-CH-021.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-021.description: The Shang (Yin) Dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) pioneered bronze metallurgy, oracle bone divination, ancestor worship, and developed the first Chinese writing system.

EA-CH-022.name: Yellow River Civilization
EA-CH-022.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-022.description: The cradle of Chinese civilization along the Yellow River (Huang He), with loess soil and river flooding supporting millet agriculture and dense settlement from Neolithic times.

EA-CH-023.name: Yangtze River Civilization
EA-CH-023.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-023.description: Rice-cultivating cultures of the Yangtze basin, including Hemudu and Majiabang, parallel and eventually merging with Yellow River civilizations to form Chinese culture.

EA-CH-024.name: Silk Production in Ancient China
EA-CH-024.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-024.description: China invented sericulture and silk weaving, with silk becoming a primary trade good and diplomatic gift. The secret of silk production gave China a trade monopoly for millennia.

EA-CH-025.name: Oracle Bones (Jiaguwen)
EA-CH-025.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-025.description: Inscribed turtle shells and ox scapulae used for divination during the Shang Dynasty, the earliest known Chinese writing, providing records of royal rituals, wars, and weather.

EA-JP-001.name: Japanese Creation Myth: Chaos and the Beginning
EA-JP-001.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-001.description: In the beginning, there was no shape to the world, only a swirling chaos. From this shapeless mass, a light rose and the first divine beings were born. The myth establishes Japan as a land formed by divine will.

EA-JP-002.name: Izanagi and Izanami
EA-JP-002.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-002.description: The divine couple tasked with creating the Japanese islands. Standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven, they stirred the ocean with a jeweled spear, drops forming the first island Onogoro. Their union gave birth to the Japanese archipelago.

EA-JP-003.name: Amaterasu, Sun Goddess
EA-JP-003.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-003.description: Born from Izanagi's left eye as he washed in a river after escaping the underworld, Amaterasu became the supreme goddess of the sun and the divine ancestor of Japan's imperial line.

EA-JP-004.name: Susanoo, Storm God
EA-JP-004.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-004.description: Izanagi's son born from his nose, god of storms and the sea. His destructive behavior drove Amaterasu to hide in the Ama-no-Iwato cave, plunging the world into darkness until the other gods lured her out.

EA-JP-005.name: Ama-no-Iwato Cave Myth
EA-JP-005.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-005.description: When Amaterasu hid in the heavenly cave in grief at Susanoo's rampages, the world fell into darkness. The goddess Ame-no-Uzume performed a comedic dance to lure her out, restoring sunlight to the world.

EA-JP-006.name: Yomi, the Land of the Dead
EA-JP-006.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-006.description: Izanagi descended to the underworld to retrieve Izanami, only to find her decayed. Fleeing her wrath, he blocked the entrance with a boulder, establishing the boundary between life and death.

EA-JP-007.name: Three Sacred Treasures
EA-JP-007.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-007.description: The Imperial Regalia of Japan: the Yata no Kagami (mirror, with Amaterasu), the Kusanagi no Tsurugi (sword, from Susanoo), and the Yasakani no Magatama (jewel). They legitimize the Emperor's divine rule.

EA-JP-008.name: Jimmu, First Emperor
EA-JP-008.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-008.description: Mythical first emperor of Japan, descended from Amaterasu, said to have founded the Japanese state in 660 BCE. His legendary campaign from Hyuga to Yamato established the imperial line.

EA-JP-009.name: Shinto Origins
EA-JP-009.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-009.description: Shinto, the indigenous religion of Japan, means "the way of the gods." It reverences kami (sacred spirits) in natural features and ancestors, with practices including shrine worship, ritual purification, and seasonal festivals.

EA-JP-010.name: Jomon Period
EA-JP-010.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-010.description: Japan's Neolithic era (c. 14,000-300 BCE) named for cord-marked pottery, marked by hunter-gatherer-fisher lifestyles, pit dwellings, and the earliest pottery in the world.

EA-JP-011.name: Yayoi Period
EA-JP-011.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-011.description: Period (c. 300 BCE - 300 CE) of agricultural revolution in Japan, with wet-rice cultivation, bronze and iron tool use, and the introduction of the Yayoi people from the Asian mainland.

SA-IN-001.name: Hindu Creation Myth
SA-IN-001.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-001.description: Hindu cosmology describes creation through Brahma, the creator god born from a golden cosmic egg, who emanates all existence. The Trimurti of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver), and Shiva (destroyer) sustain cosmic cycles.

SA-IN-002.name: Mauryan Empire (322-185 BCE)
SA-IN-002.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-002.description: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya, expanded by his grandson Ashoka the Great, the Mauryan Empire was the first pan-Indian empire, withstanding Hellenistic contact and converting Ashoka to Buddhism.

SA-IN-003.name: Ashoka the Great
SA-IN-003.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-003.description: Third Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE) who famously converted to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga War. His rock edicts spread Buddhist ethics across India and remain among the earliest written Indic records.

SA-IN-004.name: Gupta Empire (320-550 CE)
SA-IN-004.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-004.description: The Gupta period is considered a golden age of India, marked by advances in mathematics (the concept of zero, the decimal system), astronomy, literature (Kalidasa), and the consolidation of Hindu and Buddhist culture.

SA-IN-005.name: Kushan Empire
SA-IN-005.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-005.description: The Kushan Empire (c. 30-375 CE) spanned Central Asia and northern India, connecting China, India, and Rome. It patronized Buddhism and produced the Gandharan artistic style blending Greek and Indian elements.

EA-KR-001.name: Korean Foundation Myth
EA-KR-001.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-001.description: Dangun myth: Hwanung descended from heaven to live with a bear-turned-woman, founding Gojoseon in 2333 BCE, Korea's first kingdom. The myth establishes the peninsula's ancient identity.

CA-ST-001.name: Steppe Geography
CA-ST-001.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-001.description: The Eurasian Steppe is a vast grassland stretching from Manchuria to Europe, home to nomadic peoples whose mobility (horseback riding) created recurrent pressure on settled civilizations to the south.

CA-ST-002.name: Bronze Age Steppe Cultures
CA-ST-002.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-002.description: Sintashta-Petrovka and Andronovo cultures (c. 2000-900 BCE) in the steppe pioneered early horse domestication, spoke Indo-Iranian languages, and spread chariot technology and Indo-European influence across Eurasia.

CA-ST-003.name: Xiongnu Confederacy
CA-ST-003.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-003.description: The Xiongnu were the dominant steppe power from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, harassing Chinese dynasties. They are sometimes linked to the Huns, though the connection is debated.

EA-CH-026.name: Oracle Bone Divination
EA-CH-026.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-026.description: Shang kings divined by inscribing questions on heated turtle plastrons or ox scapulae, then interpreting the resulting cracks. The process produced the earliest Chinese writing and royal archives.

EA-CH-027.name: Bronze Ritual Vessels
EA-CH-027.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-027.description: Shang and Zhou bronze vessels (ding, gui, zun) were symbols of royal and aristocratic power, used in ancestor worship rituals. Their inscriptions record events and lineages of the elite.

EA-CH-028.name: Lacquerware Tradition
EA-CH-028.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-028.description: Chinese lacquer, made from the sap of the lacquer tree, was refined over millennia into waterproof, durable coatings for vessels, weapons, and tomb objects, peaking in the Warring States and Han periods.

EA-CH-029.name: Hundred Schools of Thought Impact
EA-CH-029.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-029.description: The intellectual competition of the late Zhou produced enduring frameworks: Confucianism shaped state ideology, Daoism influenced art and mysticism, Legalism built the Qin state, Mohism influenced universalistic ethics.

EA-JP-012.name: Rice Cultivation in Yayoi
EA-JP-012.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-012.description: The introduction of wet-rice paddy agriculture from the Korean peninsula and China during the Yayoi period transformed Japanese society, enabling population growth, villages, and eventually states.

EA-JP-013.name: Kofun Tombs
EA-JP-013.domain: East Asia - Unit 1: Ancient Civilizations - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-013.description: Massive keyhole-shaped burial mounds built for elite Yamato rulers in the 4th-6th centuries, with haniwa terracotta figures. Some still survive, designated as UNESCO World Heritage sites.

EA-CH-030.name: Qin Dynasty (221-206 BCE)
EA-CH-030.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-030.description: The Qin Dynasty, founded by Qin Shihuang, was the first unified imperial dynasty of China. Its brief but transformative rule standardized writing, weights, measures, currency, and built the Great Wall.

EA-CH-031.name: Qin Shihuang, First Emperor
EA-CH-031.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-031.description: Born Ying Zheng, king of Qin who completed the conquest of the Warring States in 221 BCE. Took the title "First Emperor" (Shihuangdi), proclaimed a new dynastic system to outlast all predecessors.

EA-CH-032.name: Qin Standardization
EA-CH-032.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-032.description: Qin unified scripts, weights, measures, and currency across the former warring states, ending centuries of fragmentation. These standards continued in China for two millennia, enabling commerce and administration.

EA-CH-033.name: Great Wall of China
EA-CH-033.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-033.description: Qin connected and extended earlier state walls into a unified northern frontier defense. The Great Wall was rebuilt in stone and brick under later dynasties (notably Ming) into its iconic form.

EA-CH-034.name: Qin Roads and Canals
EA-CH-034.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-034.description: Qin built an imperial road network and canals, including early work on routes later expanded along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, facilitating military movement, trade, and tax transport.

EA-CH-035.name: Legalist State under Qin
EA-CH-035.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-035.description: The Qin rejected Confucian ritual in favor of strict Legalist governance: codified laws, collective responsibility, harsh punishments, and state control of agriculture and military service.

EA-CH-036.name: Burning of the Books
EA-CH-036.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-036.description: Qin Shihuang ordered the burning of books outside the imperial archives and buried alive 460 scholars who defied the order (213 BCE), attempting to destroy intellectual opposition and standardize thought.

EA-CH-037.name: Strengthening the Trunk, Weakening the Branches
EA-CH-037.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-037.description: Qin policy of concentrating power at the center by moving wealthy noble families from their regional power bases to the capital, preventing regional rebellion.

EA-CH-038.name: Qin Standardized Currency
EA-CH-038.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-038.description: The Qin adopted a round copper coin with a square hole (ban liang) as the universal currency, replacing the diverse currencies of the former warring states and facilitating trade.

EA-CH-039.name: Standardized Script (Small Seal)
EA-CH-039.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-039.description: Qin Li Si designed a simplified "Small Seal" script (xiaozhuan) as the official writing system, replacing the diverse scripts of the former states. This standardized written communication across the empire.

EA-CH-040.name: Han Dynasty (202 BCE - 220 CE)
EA-CH-040.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-040.description: Founded by Liu Bang, the Han Dynasty succeeded the Qin and ruled China for four centuries, expanding territory, establishing the Silk Road, and adopting Confucianism as state ideology, defining Chinese identity.

EA-CH-041.name: Silk Road Trade Network
EA-CH-041.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-041.description: The Han-era Silk Road connected China to Central Asia, India, Persia, and Rome. Silk, tea, and porcelain flowed west; horses, gold, and ideas (notably Buddhism) flowed east.

EA-CH-042.name: Civil Service Examination Origins
EA-CH-042.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-042.description: The Han formalized recommendations for office based on local reputation. The examination system would mature in later dynasties, but its Han-era roots shaped Chinese meritocratic governance.

EA-CH-043.name: Xiongnu and the Northern Frontier
EA-CH-043.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-043.description: The Xiongnu, a confederation of steppe nomads, were the chief rivals of Han China. In response to raids, the Han built walls, married princesses for peace, and eventually fought major wars of expansion.

EA-CH-044.name: Wang Mang and the Xin Dynasty
EA-CH-044.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-044.description: Wang Mang seized the throne in 9 CE, founding the short-lived Xin Dynasty, attempting radical land and currency reforms that failed and caused the chaos of the Red Eyebrows Rebellion.

EA-CH-045.name: Yellow Turban Rebellion
EA-CH-045.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-045.description: The 184 CE peasant rebellion led by Zhang Jue and the Way of Supreme Peace (Taiping Dao) religious movement, hastening the collapse of the Han Dynasty into the Three Kingdoms period.

EA-JP-014.name: Yamato Dynasty
EA-JP-014.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-014.description: The Yamato state (c. 250-710 CE) was the first centralized Japanese polity, ruling from the Yamato plain. Its chieftains claimed descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu, founding the imperial line.

EA-JP-015.name: Kabane System
EA-JP-015.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-015.description: The Yamato court organized clans into hereditary title ranks called kabane (e.g., omi, muraji, kuni no miyatsuko). This system centralized Yamato control by binding regional elites to court status.

EA-JP-016.name: Kofun Tombs and Yamato Power
EA-JP-016.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-016.description: Massive keyhole-shaped Kofun burial mounds, especially for Yamato kings, demonstrated the wealth and authority of the central rulers, including the famous Daisen Kofun (Emperor Nintoku's tomb).

EA-JP-017.name: Shinto and Yamato Authority
EA-JP-017.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-017.description: Yamato rulers claimed descent from kami, making the imperial family central to Shinto worship. Shinto shrines (jinja) became a unifying institution across Japan, with Ise Grand Shrine the most sacred.

EA-JP-018.name: Jinshin War (672 CE)
EA-JP-018.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-018.description: The Jinshin War, fought between Prince Ōtomo and Prince Ōama for the Yamato throne, was the largest conflict in ancient Japanese history, with tens of thousands of arrows fired in a single battle.

EA-JP-019.name: Taika Reforms (645 CE)
EA-JP-019.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-019.description: A series of reforms modeled on Tang China, beginning with the Taika Reform edict, established centralized imperial government, redistributed land (handen system), and created a capital at Nara (Heijō-kyō).

EA-JP-020.name: Handen System
EA-JP-020.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-020.description: The Japanese land redistribution system borrowed from Tang China, where land was theoretically owned by the state and allocated to households for cultivation, with taxes paid in rice and labor.

EA-JP-021.name: Prince Shōtoku and the Seventeen-Article Constitution
EA-JP-021.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-021.description: Prince Shōtoku (574-622) championed Chinese learning, Buddhism, and centralized rule, issuing a constitution of moral and political principles that shaped Japanese governance for centuries.

EA-JP-022.name: Asuka Period Buddhism
EA-JP-022.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-022.description: The introduction of Buddhism from Baekje (Korea) in 538 or 552 CE sparked religious and political conflict between the pro-Buddhist Soga clan and the conservative Mononobe and Nakatomi clans.

EA-JP-023.name: Nara Period (710-794)
EA-JP-023.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-023.description: The Nara period saw Japan's first permanent capital at Heijō-kyō (modern Nara), modeled on Tang Chang'an. Buddhism flourished, with the Todai-ji temple and Great Buddha as monuments.

EA-KR-002.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
EA-KR-002.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-002.description: The Korean peninsula was divided into three kingdoms from the 1st century BCE to the 7th century CE: Goguryeo (north), Baekje (southwest), and Silla (southeast), each with distinct cultures and shifting alliances.

EA-KR-003.name: Silla Unification
EA-KR-003.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-003.description: Silla, allied with Tang China, defeated Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), unifying the peninsula under the Unified Silla dynasty. Chinese cultural influence peaked during this period.

EA-KR-004.name: Goguryeo Kingdom
EA-KR-004.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-004.description: The northern Korean kingdom (37 BCE - 668 CE) was known for military strength, resistance against Tang China, and its founding myth of Jumong. Its tomb murals depict daily life and cosmology.

CA-ST-004.name: Silk Road Caravanserai
CA-ST-004.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-004.description: Along the Silk Road, caravanserais (way stations) provided shelter, water, and trade protection for merchants traveling between China and the Mediterranean, becoming cosmopolitan centers of exchange.

CA-ST-005.name: Buddhism Spreads Along the Silk Road
CA-ST-005.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-005.description: Buddhism traveled from India to China via Central Asian oasis cities, with Gandhara (modern Pakistan/Afghanistan) as a key transmission zone where Greek and Indian artistic traditions merged.

EA-CH-046.name: Han Confucianism
EA-CH-046.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-046.description: Emperor Wu of Han (r. 141-87 BCE) established Confucianism as state ideology, founding the Imperial Academy and adopting Dong Zhongshu's synthesis of Confucian ethics with cosmological theories.

EA-CH-047.name: Three Kingdoms Period (220-280 CE)
EA-CH-047.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-047.description: After the Han collapse, China divided into Wei, Shu, and Wu kingdoms, dramatized in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms. The period ended with Jin unification, followed by further fragmentation.

EA-CH-048.name: Jin Dynasty (266-420 CE)
EA-CH-048.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-048.description: The Western Jin briefly unified China after the Three Kingdoms, but was disrupted by the Wu Hu uprising of non-Han peoples from the north, leading to the Southern and Northern Dynasties period.

EA-CH-049.name: Southern and Northern Dynasties (420-589 CE)
EA-CH-049.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-049.description: Centuries of division between Han Chinese in the south and various non-Han dynasties in the north, marked by Buddhism's rise, technological innovation, and gradual sinicization of steppe peoples.

EA-JP-024.name: Yamato Decline
EA-JP-024.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-024.description: By the late 6th century, the Yamato court faced aristocratic power struggles, social unrest, and continental threats. The Soga clan's embrace of Buddhism shifted political and cultural dynamics.

EA-KR-005.name: Baekje Kingdom
EA-KR-005.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-005.description: The southwest Korean kingdom (18 BCE - 660 CE) was a major maritime power, transmitting Buddhism, Chinese writing, and advanced culture to Japan. Its fall to Silla-Tang forces ended its role as a cultural intermediary.

CA-ST-006.name: Silk Road Decline and Revival
CA-ST-006.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-006.description: Political instability in Central Asia and the rise of maritime trade routes periodically disrupted the Silk Road. It revived under Tang protection and during the Mongol Empire's Pax Mongolica.

EA-CH-050.name: Han Bureaucracy
EA-CH-050.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-050.description: The Han developed a sophisticated bureaucracy of 130,000 officials serving 60 million people, organized into nine ranks, with salaries in grain and promotions based on meritorious service.

EA-CH-051.name: Daoism in the Han
EA-CH-051.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-051.description: Han-era Daoism matured from philosophical Daoism (Laozi, Zhuangzi) into religious Daoism, with celestial masters, talismans, alchemy, and the search for immortality, sometimes leading to popular unrest.

EA-JP-025.name: Jinshin War and Centralization
EA-JP-025.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-025.description: The Jinshin War's outcome enabled the centralization of Yamato rule, the codification of court ranks, and the promotion of Buddhism as state religion, accelerating Japan's adoption of continental institutions.

EA-CH-052.name: Buddhism Enters China
EA-CH-052.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-052.description: Buddhism reached China via the Silk Road in the 1st century CE, initially regarded as a foreign religion. It gained imperial patronage in the 4th-5th centuries and became integral to Chinese spiritual life.

EA-CH-053.name: Wang Mang Reforms
EA-CH-053.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-053.description: Wang Mang (r. 9-23 CE) nationalized land, replaced currency, and reorganized the bureaucracy. The Xin Dynasty's collapse from peasant revolts demonstrated the limits of radical reform without elite support.

EA-CH-054.name: Han Decline and Three Kingdoms
EA-CH-054.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-054.description: The late Han saw eunuch factions, land concentration, and peasant rebellions. The Yellow Turban Rebellion (184 CE) shattered central authority, leading to the Three Kingdoms division (220-280 CE).

EA-JP-026.name: Chinese Writing Adopted in Japan
EA-JP-026.domain: East Asia - Unit 2: Centralization and Rise of Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-026.description: Chinese characters (kanji) were adopted for Japanese writing, initially to record Chinese-language documents, then adapted for Japanese phonology via man'yōgana and eventually kana syllabaries.

EA-CH-060.name: Sui Dynasty (581-618 CE)
EA-CH-060.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-060.description: The short-lived Sui Dynasty reunified China after nearly four centuries of division, ending the Southern and Northern Dynasties period. It rebuilt the Great Wall, reconnected the Silk Road, and began the Grand Canal connecting the Yellow and Yangtze rivers.

EA-CH-061.name: Grand Canal of China
EA-CH-061.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-061.description: Begun under the Sui and expanded under the Tang and Song, the Grand Canal ran over 1,100 miles from Beijing to Hangzhou, the longest artificial waterway in the world, linking northern political centers with southern economic resources.

EA-CH-062.name: Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE)
EA-CH-062.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-062.description: Founded by Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu), the Tang Dynasty presided over a cosmopolitan golden age of poetry, painting, sculpture, and international trade, with Chang'an as the world's largest city and a hub of Silk Road exchange.

EA-CH-063.name: Emperor Taizong of Tang
EA-CH-063.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-063.description: Tang Taizong (r. 626-649) is considered one of China's greatest emperors, consolidating imperial power, defeating the Eastern Turks, expanding into Central Asia, and sponsoring the monk Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India.

EA-CH-064.name: Wu Zetian, Only Female Emperor
EA-CH-064.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-064.description: Wu Zetian (r. 690-705) was the only woman in Chinese history to claim the title of emperor, ruling the Zhou Dynasty interregnum within the Tang. She promoted Buddhism, expanded the civil service, and broke many gender barriers.

EA-CH-065.name: Tang Poetry and Li Bai
EA-CH-065.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-065.description: The Tang Dynasty is the golden age of Chinese poetry, with Li Bai (Li Po, 701-762) and Du Fu (712-770) towering figures. Li Bai's romantic, Taoist-inspired poems about wine, moon, and friendship remain among China's most beloved works.

EA-CH-066.name: Tang Buddhism: Pure Land and Chan
EA-CH-066.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-066.description: Tang Buddhism matured into distinct schools, including Pure Land (jingtu, popular devotion to Amitabha Buddha) and Chan (Zen, meditation-focused). These schools spread to Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

EA-CH-067.name: Xuanzang and the Journey to the West
EA-CH-067.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-067.description: The Tang monk Xuanzang (602-664) traveled to India via the Silk Road (629-645), returning with Buddhist scriptures that he translated into Chinese. His journey inspired the classic novel Journey to the West.

EA-CH-068.name: An Lushan Rebellion
EA-CH-068.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-068.description: The 755-763 CE An Lushan Rebellion devastated the Tang Dynasty, killing tens of millions and forcing population flight southward. The dynasty survived but never recovered its early vigor, beginning its long decline.

EA-CH-069.name: Tang Equal-Field System
EA-CH-069.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-069.description: The Tang equal-field system allocated state land to households based on labor capacity, with periodic redistribution. The system's breakdown, as land concentrated in elite hands, contributed to Tang decline.

EA-CH-070.name: Tang Two-Tax System
EA-CH-070.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-070.description: Implemented in 780 CE, the Two-Tax System replaced the equal-field system with taxes paid in summer and autumn based on property. It marked a shift to monetized taxation and private land ownership.

EA-CH-071.name: Foot Binding Origins
EA-CH-071.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-071.description: Foot binding began in the late Tang or early Song, eventually becoming a widespread practice binding girls' feet to small sizes. The custom symbolized elite status, restricted women's mobility, and persisted into the 20th century.

EA-CH-072.name: Song Dynasty (960-1279 CE)
EA-CH-072.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-072.description: The Song Dynasty reunified most of China and presided over a commercial, urban, and technological revolution. The Song saw the world's first paper money, gunpowder weapons, the compass for navigation, and movable-type printing.

EA-CH-073.name: Song Economic Revolution
EA-CH-073.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-073.description: The Song period saw a dramatic boom in rice agriculture (with new Champa rice varieties), urbanization (with cities of 1+ million), and commercialization. China's GDP per capita was among the world's highest.

EA-CH-074.name: Champa Rice and Agricultural Revolution
EA-CH-074.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-074.description: New fast-ripening Champa rice from Vietnam allowed double-cropping in southern China, dramatically increasing food production. The Song population doubled to over 100 million, supported by this agricultural revolution.

EA-CH-075.name: Song Paper Money (Jiaozi)
EA-CH-075.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-075.description: The Song invented the world's first government-issued paper money (jiaozi), facilitating long-distance trade. The system eventually suffered inflation, but the concept of fiat currency spread along the Silk Road.

EA-CH-076.name: Song Gunpowder and Firearms
EA-CH-076.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-076.description: The Song developed gunpowder weapons including fire lances, bombs, and early firearms. Military pressure from northern nomads (Khitan, Jurchen) drove this arms race, with gunpowder technology eventually reaching the Islamic world and Europe.

EA-CH-077.name: Movable-Type Printing (Bi Sheng)
EA-CH-077.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-077.description: Around 1040 CE, the Song artisan Bi Sheng invented movable-type printing using fired clay characters, a millennium before Gutenberg. Initially less practical for Chinese with thousands of characters, the invention was crucial for Korea and later Europe.

EA-CH-078.name: Song Compass for Navigation
EA-CH-078.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-078.description: The Song perfected the magnetic compass for ocean navigation, enabling the great trading fleets of the Song and Ming. Chinese compass technology reached Arab and European navigators by the 12th century.

EA-CH-079.name: Marco Polo in Song China
EA-CH-079.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-079.description: The Italian merchant Marco Polo claimed to have served Kublai Khan's Yuan court (1275-1292), describing Hangzhou as "the finest and most splendid city in the world." His account introduced Europeans to East Asian wealth and sophistication.

EA-CH-080.name: Southern Song Capital Lin'an (Hangzhou)
EA-CH-080.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-080.description: After losing the north to the Jurchen Jin, the Song court re-established itself at Lin'an (modern Hangzhou), a cosmopolitan port and commercial hub. Marco Polo called it "Quinsai," the finest city in the world.

EA-CH-081.name: Song Civil Service Examinations
EA-CH-081.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-081.description: The Song expanded the civil service examination system dramatically, opening paths to office for commoners. Examinations tested mastery of Confucian classics, with essay-style questions on policy and moral reasoning.

EA-CH-082.name: Song Landscape Painting
EA-CH-082.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-082.description: Song landscape painting (shanshui) reached sublime heights, with artists like Fan Kuan, Guo Xi, and Ma Yuan creating monumental mountain-and-water compositions expressing cosmic and moral order.

EA-CH-083.name: Neo-Confucianism and Zhu Xi
EA-CH-083.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-083.description: The Song Neo-Confucian synthesis, especially by Zhu Xi (1130-1200), reinterpreted Confucianism through Daoist and Buddhist concepts, emphasizing the investigation of things (gewu) and the principle (li) underlying the universe.

EA-CH-084.name: Song Iron and Steel Production
EA-CH-084.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-084.description: The Song dramatically increased iron and steel production, with annual output reaching 125,000 tons by 1078 CE, larger than all of Europe combined. Steel was used for tools, weapons, and agricultural implements.

EA-CH-085.name: Northern Song Fall to Jurchen
EA-CH-085.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-085.description: In 1127 CE the Jurchen Jin captured the Northern Song capital Kaifeng in the Jingkang Incident, seizing Emperor Huizong and much of the imperial family. The remnants fled south, founding the Southern Song.

EA-CH-086.name: Song Maritime Trade
EA-CH-086.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-086.description: The Song developed a massive maritime trade network, with Chinese junks sailing to Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, and East Africa. Quanzhou and Guangzhou became among the world's busiest ports.

EA-JP-027.name: Heian Period (794-1185)
EA-JP-027.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-027.description: The Heian period, named for the capital Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto), saw the flowering of classical Japanese culture: court poetry, monogatari (tales), and the rise of aristocratic Fujiwara rule.

EA-JP-028.name: Lady Murasaki and The Tale of Genji
EA-JP-028.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-028.description: Murasaki Shikibu, a Heian court lady, wrote The Tale of Genji (c. 1010), often considered the world's first novel. The work depicts court life, romance, and Buddhist themes with psychological depth.

EA-JP-029.name: Heian Aristocratic Culture
EA-JP-029.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-029.description: Heian aristocratic culture prized aesthetic refinement, poetry, calligraphy, and romantic love. Men wrote in Chinese; women developed kana script and produced much of the era's great literature.

EA-JP-030.name: Fujiwara Regency Politics
EA-JP-030.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-030.description: The Fujiwara clan dominated Heian politics by marrying their daughters to emperors, then serving as regents (sesshō) for child emperors. This system concentrated real power in the Fujiwara for over a century.

EA-JP-031.name: Taira-Minamoto War (Genpei War)
EA-JP-031.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-031.description: The 1180-1185 Genpei War between the Taira and Minamoto clans ended aristocratic Heian rule. Minamoto no Yoritomo established the Kamakura Shogunate, beginning samurai dominance of Japan.

EA-JP-032.name: Minamoto no Yoritomo
EA-JP-032.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-032.description: Founder of the Kamakura Shogunate and first shogun (1192), Yoritomo established the samurai-dominated feudal system that would govern Japan for nearly 700 years.

EA-JP-033.name: The Pillow Book (Sei Shōnagon)
EA-JP-033.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-033.description: Heian lady Sei Shōnagon's The Pillow Book (c. 1002) is a witty, observational miscellany of court life, famous for its lists, aesthetic judgments, and self-aware literary criticism.

EA-JP-034.name: Bugaku Court Dance and Music
EA-JP-034.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-034.description: Bugaku, the imperial court's elegant dance and music tradition, blended Tang Chinese, Korean, Indian, and Southeast Asian elements. It remains performed at the Japanese imperial court today.

EA-KR-006.name: Goryeo Dynasty (918-1392)
EA-KR-006.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-006.description: Founded by Wang Geon, the Goryeo Dynasty unified Korea, gave its name to "Korea" in Western languages, and produced celadon pottery, the Tripitaka Koreana (Buddhist scriptures carved on 80,000 woodblocks), and metal movable type.

EA-KR-007.name: Goryeo Celadon
EA-KR-007.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-007.description: Goryeo celadon, a jade-green glazed pottery, was prized throughout East Asia. Goryeo potters developed unique sanggam inlay techniques using white and black slip beneath the glaze to create elegant motifs.

EA-KR-008.name: Tripitaka Koreana
EA-KR-008.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-008.description: Carved on over 80,000 woodblocks during the Mongol invasion (1236-1251), the Tripitaka Koreana is the most complete Buddhist canon in existence, preserved at Haeinsa Temple. It is a UNESCO Memory of the World.

EA-KR-009.name: Korean Metal Movable Type
EA-KR-009.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-009.description: In 1234, during the Goryeo Dynasty, Koreans invented metal movable type, predating Gutenberg by over 200 years. Earlier, Bi Sheng's clay type (China, c. 1040) had been less practical for Chinese characters.

EA-KR-010.name: Korean Confucianism and Joseon Origins
EA-KR-010.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-010.description: The Goryeo's adoption of Neo-Confucianism, especially through the writings of Jeong Jeong-si and An Hyang, prepared the way for the Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910) and its rigid Confucian state ideology.

SA-IN-006.name: Chola Empire (848-1279 CE)
SA-IN-006.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-006.description: The Chola Dynasty of southern India became a major maritime power, controlling trade with Southeast Asia and projecting power as far as the Srivijaya kingdom of Sumatra. Their bronze sculpture reached extraordinary heights.

SA-IN-007.name: Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526 CE)
SA-IN-007.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-007.description: The Delhi Sultanate was the first major Islamic state in India, founded by Muhammad of Ghor's slave-general Qutb al-Din Aibak. Five successive dynasties ruled from Delhi, blending Persian and Indian cultures.

SA-IN-008.name: Qutb Minar
SA-IN-008.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-008.description: Begun in 1199 by Qutb al-Din Aibak, the Qutb Minar is a 73-meter fluted red sandstone minaret in Delhi, marking the site of the first Muslim conquest of India. Its construction continued across multiple sultanate dynasties.

SA-IN-009.name: Bhakti Movement
SA-IN-009.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-009.description: The Bhakti movement (6th-17th centuries) emphasized personal devotion to a deity, often Krishna or Shiva, rejecting caste barriers. Saints like Kabir, Mirabai, and Ramananda made devotional Hinduism accessible across social lines.

SA-IN-010.name: South Indian Temple Architecture
SA-IN-010.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-010.description: South Indian Dravidian temple architecture, seen in the Brihadishvara (Thanjavur) and Meenakshi (Madurai) temples, featured towering gopurams, mandapas, and extensive sculptural programs, with temples as civic and economic centers.

CA-ST-007.name: Turkic Migrations
CA-ST-007.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-007.description: Turkic peoples from the Altai and steppe regions spread westward and southward from the 6th century CE, forming the Göktürk, Uyghur, and later Kipchak khanates. Their migrations reshaped Central Asian and Middle Eastern demographics.

CA-ST-008.name: Göktürk Khaganate
CA-ST-008.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-008.description: The Göktürk (Celestial Turks) Khaganate (552-744 CE) was the first major Turkic state, controlling much of the Eurasian steppe. The Orkhon inscriptions are among the earliest known Turkic-language texts.

CA-ST-009.name: Uyghur Khaganate
CA-ST-009.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-009.description: The Uyghur Khaganate (744-840 CE) succeeded the Göktürk in Mongolia, later migrating to the Turfan region in modern Xinjiang, where they established a kingdom blending Turkic, Chinese, and Tocharian Buddhist cultures.

CA-ST-010.name: Khitan Liao Dynasty
CA-ST-010.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-010.description: The Khitan Liao Dynasty (907-1125), founded by the Khitan nomads, controlled parts of Manchuria, Mongolia, and northern China. The Liao ruled a dual administration governing both nomadic and sedentary populations separately.

EA-CH-087.name: Chinese Maritime Silk Road
EA-CH-087.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-087.description: Song maritime trade extended the Silk Road into the seas, with Chinese porcelain, silk, and tea exchanged for spices, ivory, gems, and precious metals from Southeast Asia, India, Persia, and East Africa.

EA-CH-088.name: Hangzhou and Song Urbanization
EA-CH-088.domain: East Asia - Unit 3: Golden Ages - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-088.description: Hangzhou (Lin'an) was the Song capital and one of the world's largest cities, with a population over 1 million. Its canals, markets, restaurants, and entertainment quarters astonished foreign visitors like Marco Polo.

CA-ST-011.name: Steppe Nomadic Lifestyle
CA-ST-011.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-011.description: Eurasian steppe nomads herded horses, sheep, goats, and cattle across vast grasslands. Their mobility, horsemanship, and composite bows made them formidable raiders and conquerors of settled civilizations to the south.

CA-ST-012.name: Nomadic Raids vs Settled Empires
CA-ST-012.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-012.description: At first, steppe nomads raided settled civilizations for plunder, capturing cities, stealing goods, then withdrawing. This changed as they built nomadic empires that ruled over both steppe and agricultural populations.

CA-ST-013.name: Northern Wei Dynasty (386-534 CE)
CA-ST-013.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-013.description: The Northern Wei, founded by the Tuoba Xianbei, ruled northern China and sponsored Buddhist cave art at Yungang and Longmen. Their Sinicization policies under Emperor Xiaowen (494 CE) prompted cultural reform but also resistance.

CA-ST-014.name: Liao Dynasty (907-1125 CE)
CA-ST-014.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-014.description: The Khitan Liao Dynasty ruled a vast empire across Manchuria, Mongolia, and parts of northern China, administering nomadic and sedentary populations through parallel institutions. The Liao were eventually destroyed by their former Jurchen vassals.

CA-ST-015.name: Jin Dynasty (1115-1234 CE)
CA-ST-015.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-015.description: Founded by the Jurchen Wanyan clan, the Jin Dynasty captured the Northern Song capital Kaifeng in 1127 (Jingkang Incident), forcing the Song to flee south. The Jin ruled northern China until destroyed by the Mongols.

CA-ST-016.name: Jurchen People and the Eight Banners
CA-ST-016.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-016.description: The Jurchen were a Tungusic people of northeastern Manchuria. Nurhaci organized them into the Eight Banners system (1615), a military-administrative structure that would carry the Manchus to conquer China in 1644.

CA-ST-017.name: Nurhaci and the Manchu State
CA-ST-017.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-017.description: Nurhaci (1559-1626) unified Jurchen clans into a Manchu identity, founded the Later Jin (1616), and created the Eight Banners. His son Hong Taiji renamed the dynasty Qing in 1636.

CA-ST-018.name: Mongol Tribes and Temujin
CA-ST-018.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-018.description: In the late 12th century, the Mongol tribes of the steppe were fragmented and warring. Temujin (Genghis Khan) unified them by 1206, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.

CA-ST-019.name: Genghis Khan (1162-1227)
CA-ST-019.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-019.description: Born Temujin, he unified the Mongol tribes (1206), took the title Genghis Khan ("Universal Ruler"), and launched campaigns that conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia, and eastern Europe, founding the Mongol Empire.

CA-ST-020.name: Mongol Military Tactics
CA-ST-020.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-020.description: The Mongol military combined superb horsemanship, the composite bow, feigned retreats, psychological terror, and effective intelligence networks. Their decimal organization (units of 10, 100, 1000, 10,000) enabled rapid coordinated campaigns.

CA-ST-021.name: Mongol Conquest of Jin
CA-ST-021.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-021.description: Genghis Khan and his son Ögedei conquered the Jurchen Jin Dynasty by 1234, devastating northern China. The campaign featured the siege of Zhongdu (Beijing) and the controversial use of conquered populations as siege troops.

CA-ST-022.name: Mongol Conquest of Khwarezm
CA-ST-022.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-022.description: In 1219-1221, Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarezmian Empire in retaliation for the murder of his envoys, systematically destroying cities like Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv, and Urgench, and opening Central Asia to Mongol rule.

CA-ST-023.name: Ögedei Khan and Mongol Expansion
CA-ST-023.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-023.description: Ögedei Khan (r. 1229-1241) presided over the Mongol Empire's greatest expansion, completing the conquest of northern China, invading Russia and Eastern Europe, and reaching the gates of Vienna and the Adriatic.

CA-ST-024.name: Kublai Khan and the Yuan Dynasty
CA-ST-024.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-024.description: Kublai Khan (r. 1260-1294) completed the conquest of southern China, founding the Yuan Dynasty (1271). He moved the capital to Khanbaliq (Beijing), patronized Tibetan Buddhism, and welcomed foreign travelers like Marco Polo.

CA-ST-025.name: Pax Mongolica
CA-ST-025.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-025.description: The Pax Mongolica was a century of relative peace and prosperity across Eurasia (c. 1250-1350), enabling unprecedented travel and trade along the Silk Road. Goods, technologies, ideas, and unfortunately the Black Death spread along Mongol-protected routes.

CA-ST-026.name: Mongol Administration and Yam System
CA-ST-026.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-026.description: The Mongols governed their vast empire through the Yam postal relay system and a multicultural bureaucracy incorporating Chinese, Persian, Uighur, and Mongol administrators. The system unified Eurasian trade and communication.

CA-ST-027.name: Sack of Baghdad (1258)
CA-ST-027.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-027.description: Hulagu Khan's Mongol army sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate. The destruction of libraries and the killing of the last Abbasid caliph symbolized the catastrophic end of the Islamic Golden Age's political center.

CA-ST-028.name: Mongol Invasions of Japan
CA-ST-028.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-028.description: Kublai Khan attempted to invade Japan in 1274 and 1281, both fleets destroyed by typhoons the Japanese called kamikaze ("divine wind"). The invasions shaped Japanese xenophobia and military culture for centuries.

CA-ST-029.name: Mongol Cultural Exchange
CA-ST-029.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-029.description: The Mongol era transferred gunpowder, paper money, astronomical instruments, and printing technology from East Asia westward, while introducing Persian astronomy, Muslim cartography, and Islamic art to China.

CA-ST-030.name: Mongol Decline and Fragmentation
CA-ST-030.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-030.description: After Kublai Khan, the unified Mongol Empire fragmented into khanates: the Yuan (China), the Ilkhanate (Persia), the Golden Horde (Russia), and the Chagatai Khanate (Central Asia), each pursuing its own path.

CA-ST-031.name: Tamerlane and the Timurid Empire
CA-ST-031.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-031.description: Tamerlane (1336-1405), a Turco-Mongol conqueror based in Samarkand, built a short-lived empire from Delhi to Anatolia, sacked cities from Isfahan to Aleppo, and patronized architecture and learning. The Timurid legacy deeply influenced Mughal India.

CA-ST-032.name: Mongol Legacy in Russia
CA-ST-032.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-032.description: The Golden Horde's two-century rule (1240s-1480) shaped Russia: the rise of Moscow as a tax collector, isolation from Western Europe, and adoption of cavalry-based military culture that would persist into modern times.

EA-CH-089.name: Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368)
EA-CH-089.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-089.description: Founded by Kublai Khan, the Yuan Dynasty was the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China. It maintained Mongol privileges, patronized Tibetan Buddhism, expanded the Grand Canal, and used paper money extensively before inflation.

EA-CH-090.name: Yuan Drama and Literature
EA-CH-090.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-090.description: The Yuan Dynasty saw the flowering of Chinese opera (zaju), with playwrights like Guan Hanqing producing hundreds of plays mixing music, dance, and dialogue, performed in public theaters for diverse audiences.

EA-CH-091.name: Red Turban Rebellion
EA-CH-091.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-091.description: The 1351-1368 Red Turban Rebellion, combining religious millenarianism with peasant grievances, toppled the Yuan Dynasty. Zhu Yuanzhang, a rebel leader, founded the Ming Dynasty in 1368.

EA-CH-092.name: Mongol Influence on Ming
EA-CH-092.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-092.description: The Ming Dynasty's founder Zhu Yuanzhang came from a poor peasant background, partly a reaction to Yuan-era social disruption. Ming policies emphasized agricultural restoration, anti-nomadic defense, and strong centralization.

EA-JP-035.name: Kamakura Shogunate (1185-1333)
EA-JP-035.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-035.description: The Kamakura Shogunate, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo, was Japan's first military government. Power shifted to the Hōjō regents (shikken) after 1199. The regime ended when Emperor Go-Daigo attempted to restore imperial rule.

EA-JP-036.name: Samurai Code of Bushidō
EA-JP-036.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-036.description: Bushidō ("the way of the warrior") evolved in Kamakura Japan, emphasizing loyalty, martial honor, frugality, and readiness to die. It would be formalized in later centuries as Japan's samurai ethical code.

EA-JP-037.name: Mongol Invasions and Divine Wind
EA-JP-037.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-037.description: The Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 ended in the destruction of the invasion fleets by typhoons, the "kamikaze" (divine winds). The defense required coastal fortifications and prompted loyalty among regional warriors to the shogunate.

EA-JP-038.name: Kamakura Buddhism
EA-JP-038.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-038.description: Kamakura-era Buddhism saw the rise of new schools: Pure Land (Jōdo, salvation through Amida Buddha) and Zen (meditation). These offered hope to ordinary people in a turbulent age and shaped Japanese religious life.

EA-JP-039.name: Hōjō Regency
EA-JP-039.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-039.description: The Hōjō clan ruled as regents (shikken) for the Kamakura shoguns from 1199 to 1333, exercising real power. Their failure to pay samurai for the Mongol defense contributed to the regime's fall.

EA-JP-040.name: Emperor Go-Daigo and Kenmu Restoration
EA-JP-040.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-040.description: Emperor Go-Daigo (r. 1318-1339) briefly restored imperial rule (1333-1336) before being overthrown by Ashikaga Takauji, who established the Muromachi Shogunate.

CA-ST-033.name: Mongol Impact on Korea
CA-ST-033.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-033.description: Mongol invasions of Korea (1231-1270) devastated the Goryeo kingdom, which eventually became a Mongol vassal. Goryeo kings married Mongol princesses, and many Korean technologies (printing, pottery) influenced Yuan China.

CA-ST-034.name: Mongol Impact on Southeast Asia
CA-ST-034.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-034.description: Mongol invasions of Vietnam, Burma, and Java (13th-14th centuries) were largely unsuccessful but established tribute relationships, transferred military technology, and encouraged the rise of more militarized Southeast Asian states.

CA-ST-035.name: Mongol-Mongol Wars
CA-ST-035.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-035.description: Civil wars among Mongol khanates (Kublai vs. Ariq Böke, the Toluid Civil War) and the subsequent Ilkhanate-Golden Horde conflicts (1290s-1330s) drained the empire's strength and enabled resistance movements to flourish.

CA-ST-036.name: Rise of the Ming against the Mongols
CA-ST-036.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-036.description: The Ming founder Zhu Yuanzhang built a Han Chinese coalition to expel the Mongols in 1368, launching the "Restoration of the Ming" (ming yi). Subsequent Ming campaigns pushed Mongols into the northern steppe.

EA-KR-011.name: Korea under Mongol Influence
EA-KR-011.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-011.description: Goryeo survived the Mongol invasions by becoming a vassal, with kings marrying Mongol princesses. This preserved Korean autonomy but incorporated Mongol customs, technology, and a significant Mongol-descended aristocracy.

EA-KR-012.name: Goryeo-Mongol Royal Marriages
EA-KR-012.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-012.description: Goryeo kings married Mongol princesses, blending the royal lines. Princess Bukeokseon, daughter of Kublai Khan, married King Chungnyeol, and her descendants formed a significant segment of the later Joseon aristocracy.

CA-ST-037.name: Mongol Yuan Paper Money
CA-ST-037.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-037.description: The Yuan Dynasty issued large quantities of paper money (chao), which initially facilitated trade but eventually caused severe inflation. This experiment demonstrated both the power and limits of fiat currency.

CA-ST-038.name: Mongol Religious Patronage
CA-ST-038.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-038.description: The Mongols were religiously tolerant, patronizing Tibetan Buddhism, Nestorian Christianity, Islam, and Daoism. Tibetan lamas like Phagpa served as imperial preceptors, shaping Mongol religious politics.

CA-ST-039.name: Mongol Postal Relay (Yam)
CA-ST-039.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-039.description: The Yam system established relay stations every 25-30 miles across the empire, with horses, food, and shelter for imperial messengers and travelers. The system enabled rapid communication and administration.

EA-CH-093.name: Yuan Social Hierarchy
EA-CH-093.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-093.description: Yuan society was divided into four classes: Mongols at the top, then Semu (allied Central Asians), then Han Chinese (including northern Chinese), and at the bottom Southerners. This hierarchy created lasting resentment.

CA-ST-040.name: Mongol Empire's Largest Extent
CA-ST-040.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-040.description: At its height under Möngke Khan (r. 1251-1259), the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe, from Siberia to the Persian Gulf, covering about 24 million km², the largest contiguous land empire in history.

CA-ST-041.name: Mongol Use of Conquered Specialists
CA-ST-041.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-041.description: The Mongols systematically recruited engineers, physicians, scribes, and administrators from conquered peoples, regardless of ethnicity. This meritocratic recruitment allowed them to govern vastly different societies effectively.

CA-ST-042.name: Mongol Demography
CA-ST-042.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-042.description: Mongol conquests caused massive population losses, possibly 30-40 million deaths in Central Asia, Persia, and China combined. Some modern historians revise these figures down, but the demographic impact was profound.

CA-ST-043.name: Mongol Empire's Lasting Impact
CA-ST-043.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-043.description: The Mongol Empire reshaped Eurasia: spreading technologies (gunpowder, printing), connecting trade routes, creating new diplomatic networks, and indirectly causing the Black Death's devastating spread in the 14th century.

CA-ST-044.name: Mongol Cultural Hybridization
CA-ST-044.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-044.description: Mongol rule produced remarkable cultural exchange: Persian Ilkhanid miniatures combining Chinese and Islamic motifs, Yuan blue-and-white porcelain influenced by Persian tastes, and Indo-Persian Mughal painting later flourishing in India.

EA-JP-041.name: Muromachi Shogunate
EA-JP-041.domain: East Asia - Unit 4: Steppe Nomadic Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-041.description: The Muromachi Shogunate (1336-1573) was established by Ashikaga Takauji in Kyoto. It ruled during an era of cultural flourishing (Noh, ink painting) but increasing samurai independence that led to the Sengoku civil war period.

EA-JP-042.name: Ashikaga Shogunate and the Rise of the Shugo
EA-JP-042.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-042.description: Ashikaga Takauji turned against Emperor Go-Daigo during the 1336 rebellion, captured Kyoto, and established the Ashikaga (Muromachi) Shogunate. From this time forward, military/samurai houses determined the fate of Japan.

EA-JP-043.name: Kamakura Shogunate Period (1185-1333)
EA-JP-043.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-043.description: The first shogunate, ruled by the Minamoto clan until 1199, then the Hōjō regents. The shogunate controlled eastern Japan, with the imperial court retaining cultural and ceremonial authority. The Mongols invaded in 1274 and 1281, both attempts repelled.

EA-JP-044.name: Muromachi Period (1336-1573)
EA-JP-044.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-044.description: The Ashikaga shogunate ruled from a Kyoto neighborhood called Muromachi. The shogun started strong but became weak as the Shugo (military governors) consolidated power in the countryside, leading to the Onin War and the Sengoku period.

EA-JP-045.name: Shogunate Comparison: Heian-Kamakura-Muromachi
EA-JP-045.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-045.description: Heian: emperor and court dominant, weak samurai. Kamakura: Minamoto/Hōjō shoguns in Kamakura, eastern Japan. Muromachi: Ashikaga in Kyoto, shugo becoming powerful. Each period saw different balances between imperial and military authority.

EA-JP-046.name: Shugo Military Governors
EA-JP-046.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-046.description: The Muromachi shogunate appointed military governors (shugo) to rule the provinces. These shugo, often from the shogun's relatives, increasingly acted independently, becoming de facto rulers of their domains.

EA-JP-047.name: Rise of the Samurai Class
EA-JP-047.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-047.description: Through the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, the samurai class grew from a small retainer force into a dominant social and political class. Their martial code (bushidō) shaped Japanese ethics, art, and governance.

EA-JP-048.name: Zen Buddhism in Muromachi Japan
EA-JP-048.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-048.description: Zen Buddhism flourished under the Ashikaga shoguns, who patronized the great Zen monasteries of Kyoto (Tenryū-ji, Kinkaku-ji, Ginkaku-ji). Zen monks imported Chinese ink painting, tea ceremony, and garden design.

EA-JP-049.name: Noh Theater and Muromachi Culture
EA-JP-049.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-049.description: Zeami and Kan'ami perfected Noh theater under Ashikaga patronage. Combining masked drama, music, and dance, Noh drew on Shinto and Buddhist themes, and remains performed as Japan's most refined classical art.

EA-JP-050.name: Muromachi Shogunate Decline
EA-JP-050.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-050.description: The Muromachi Shogunate's power declined after the Ōnin War (1467-1477), which devastated Kyoto. Provincial lords (daimyō) became independent, beginning the Sengoku period (Warring States, 1467-1615).

EA-JP-051.name: Sengoku Period (1467-1615)
EA-JP-051.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-051.description: The Warring States period saw Japan fragmented among competing daimyō, with constant warfare, castle-building, and the rise of new military technologies. The period ended with the unification by Oda, Toyotomi, and Tokugawa.

EA-CH-094.name: Ming Dynasty (1368-1644)
EA-CH-094.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-094.description: Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu Emperor), the Ming Dynasty restored Han Chinese rule after the Yuan. The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall, sent Zheng He's treasure voyages, and presided over early modern Chinese culture and economy.

EA-CH-095.name: Hongwu Emperor and Ming Founding
EA-CH-095.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-095.description: Zhu Yuanzhang rose from orphan and monk to rebel leader who expelled the Mongols in 1368. As Hongwu Emperor, he concentrated power, redistributed land, and eliminated rivals in the 1380 Hu Weiyong purge.

EA-CH-096.name: Ming Land Reforms
EA-CH-096.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-096.description: The early Ming redistributed land into the well-field system, registered households, and organized military colonies. These reforms restored agriculture but were gradually abandoned as land concentrated in elite hands.

EA-CH-097.name: Ming Agricultural Innovation
EA-CH-097.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-097.description: The Ming period saw introduction of New World crops (sweet potatoes, maize, peanuts) from the Americas via Spanish and Portuguese trade, dramatically expanding arable land and supporting population growth to 150-200 million.

EA-CH-098.name: Ming Cash Crops
EA-CH-098.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-098.description: As the Ming population grew and food supply increased, farmers shifted to cash crops like cotton, indigo, sugar cane, and silk. This commercialization stimulated markets and proto-industrialization in rural areas.

EA-CH-099.name: Ming Civil Service Examinations
EA-CH-099.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-099.description: The Ming restored the civil service examinations to their Confucian classical basis, with the eight-legged essay (baguwen) as the standard format. Exams remained the primary path to official rank and social mobility.

EA-CH-100.name: Ming Scholar-Official Class
EA-CH-100.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-100.description: The Ming scholar-official class, formed through the exams, dominated government. Local officials were appointed by the court, removable for misconduct, and held no hereditary right to their lands. This was a meritocratic ideal, imperfectly realized.

EA-CH-101.name: Ming Women's Status
EA-CH-101.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-101.description: Ming women's rights declined considerably, with strict foot binding, widow chastity cults, and the cult of virtuous wives (lienü) promoted by Neo-Confucian state ideology. Women were largely confined to domestic roles.

EA-CH-102.name: Ming Maritime Voyages: Zheng He
EA-CH-102.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-102.description: Admiral Zheng He led seven massive treasure voyages (1405-1433), reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa. The fleets of 200+ ships projected Ming power until the voyages were discontinued as costly.

EA-CH-103.name: Ming Porcelain Industry
EA-CH-103.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-103.description: The Ming perfected blue-and-white porcelain, especially at Jingdezhen, producing works for the imperial court and global export. Ming porcelain shaped ceramic traditions across Asia, the Islamic world, and Europe.

EA-CH-104.name: Ming Great Wall Reconstruction
EA-CH-104.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-104.description: The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in stone and brick (largely the form seen today) to defend against Mongol raids. The wall became a symbol of Chinese civilization, employing soldiers and garrisoned communities.

EA-CH-105.name: Ming Fall to the Manchus
EA-CH-105.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-105.description: The Ming Dynasty collapsed in 1644 under combined pressures: peasant rebellions (Li Zicheng), military defeats, fiscal crisis, and Manchu invasions from the north. The last Ming emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill, Beijing.

EA-CH-106.name: Wang Yangming and Neo-Confucianism
EA-CH-106.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-106.description: Ming philosopher Wang Yangming (1472-1529) developed the "unity of knowledge and action" doctrine, arguing that true knowledge manifests in action. His school influenced East Asian thought for centuries, including in Japan and Korea.

EA-CH-107.name: Ming Population and Economy
EA-CH-107.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-107.description: The Ming saw China's population grow from 60-80 million to 150-200 million by 1600, supported by New World crops. Urbanization, market integration, and a vibrant export economy made China the world's largest economy.

SA-IN-011.name: Mughal Empire Founding (1526)
SA-IN-011.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-011.description: Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, invaded India with gunpowder weapons and cavalry, defeating the Lodi Sultan at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and founding the Mughal Empire that would rule for 300+ years.

SA-IN-012.name: Babur, First Mughal Emperor
SA-IN-012.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-012.description: Babur (1483-1530) descended from Timur and Genghis Khan. He lost his Central Asian kingdom, conquered northern India, and wrote the Baburnama, an admired memoir of conquest, gardens, and natural history.

SA-IN-013.name: Akbar the Great (r. 1556-1605)
SA-IN-013.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-013.description: Akbar, the third Mughal emperor, consolidated the empire, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, married Hindu princesses, and created a syncretic religion (Din-i-Ilahi). His administration became a model for later Mughal rulers.

SA-IN-014.name: Akbar's Religious Tolerance
SA-IN-014.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-014.description: Akbar held interfaith debates among Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Jain, and Zoroastrian scholars, patronized all faiths, and abolished discriminatory taxes. His policies of sulh-i-kul (universal peace) sought harmony among India's diverse populations.

SA-IN-015.name: Mughal Mansabdari System
SA-IN-015.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-015.description: Mughal administrators (mansabdars) held military-administrative ranks (zat) that determined status, salary, and cavalry requirements. Mansabdars were paid in jagirs (land revenue rights), making the system dependent on land revenue.

SA-IN-016.name: Mansabdars and Jagirdars
SA-IN-016.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
