SA-IN-016.description: Mansabdars held ranks (mansab) determining status, salary, and military obligations. They were paid in jagirs (land grants), and those holding jagirs were called jagirdars. The system relied on the empire's ability to assign and reassign land.

SA-IN-017.name: Akbarnama and Mughal Painting
SA-IN-017.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-017.description: The Akbarnama, Akbar's official chronicle, was illustrated with Mughal miniature paintings blending Persian, Indian, and European styles. The atelier produced thousands of illustrations, often depicting court life and battles.

SA-IN-018.name: Mughal Architecture: Taj Mahal
SA-IN-018.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-018.description: Built by Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal (completed 1653), the Taj Mahal is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the pinnacle of Mughal architecture, blending Persian, Islamic, and Indian styles in white marble.

SA-IN-019.name: Shah Jahan and Mughal High Culture
SA-IN-019.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-019.description: Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658) presided over the cultural peak of the Mughal Empire, building the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, and Jama Masjid. His reign ended when his son Aurangzeb deposed him and confined him in Agra Fort.

SA-IN-020.name: Aurangzeb and Mughal Expansion
SA-IN-020.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-020.description: Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) expanded the empire to its greatest extent but alienated Hindus, reimposed the jizya tax, and depleted finances. His death in 1707 triggered Mughal decline and the rise of regional successor states.

SA-IN-021.name: Mughal Religious Policy
SA-IN-021.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-021.description: Mughal policy oscillated between Akbar's tolerance, Aurangzeb's Islamic orthodoxy, and various compromises. Hindu-Muslim relations shaped South Asian politics for centuries, with major consequences for the modern period.

SA-IN-022.name: Maratha Confederacy
SA-IN-022.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-022.description: The Marathas, a Hindu warrior people of the Deccan, built a confederacy under Shivaji (1630-1680) that challenged Mughal power. By 1700, they were the dominant Indian power, eventually establishing their own rule.

SA-IN-023.name: Sikh Empire and Maharaja Ranjit Singh
SA-IN-023.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-023.description: Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak (1469-1539), blended Hindu and Islamic elements. By the early 19th century, Maharaja Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls into a powerful Punjab-based empire (1801-1839).

SA-IN-024.name: Vijayanagara Empire
SA-IN-024.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-024.description: The Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646), based in southern India, successfully resisted Delhi Sultanate expansion. Its capital Hampi was one of the world's largest cities before being sacked in 1565.

CA-ST-045.name: Timurid Renaissance
CA-ST-045.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-045.description: Timur's descendants, especially Ulugh Beg and the later Timurid princes, patronized a flowering of Persian-Turkic culture in Samarkand and Herat. Their aesthetic influenced Mughal India and Ottoman Persia.

CA-ST-046.name: Mongol Conversion to Islam
CA-ST-046.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-046.description: By the 14th century, the western Mongol khanates (Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai) had converted to Islam. The Yuan in China remained Buddhist, while the northern Mongols (who would become the Oirats) maintained shamanism.

EA-CH-108.name: Ming Examination Essays (Baguwen)
EA-CH-108.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-108.description: Ming civil service exams used the eight-legged essay (baguwen), a highly stylized format requiring candidates to structure arguments in eight prescribed steps. The rigid format later drew criticism for stifling independent thought.

CA-ST-047.name: Oirat Mongols and the Steppe
CA-ST-047.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-047.description: The Oirat (western Mongol) confederation, including the Khoshut, Choros, and Dörbet, dominated the steppe after the Yuan collapse. Their conflicts with the eastern (Khalha) Mongols reshaped Central Asian politics.

EA-KR-013.name: Joseon Dynasty Founding (1392)
EA-KR-013.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-013.description: The Joseon Dynasty, founded by Yi Seong-gye (Taejo), replaced the Goryeo. Joseon adopted strict Neo-Confucianism, established the scholar-official yangban class, and would rule Korea for 500+ years.

EA-KR-014.name: Joseon Neo-Confucian State
EA-KR-014.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-014.description: Joseon adopted Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism as state orthodoxy, with the scholar-officials (yangban) dominating government. Buddhism declined; education, civil service exams, and ancestor worship defined elite culture.

EA-JP-052.name: Naga-Antoku and Samurai Honor
EA-JP-052.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-052.description: The Taira clan's defeat in the Genpei War culminated in the suicide of young Emperor Antoku and the Taira grandmother. The Tale of the Heike memorialized this as the supreme example of samurai loyalty and tragic honor.

EA-JP-053.name: Heiji Rebellion (1159-1160)
EA-JP-053.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-053.description: A minor conflict between the Taira and Minamoto clans, the Heiji Rebellion was a precursor to the larger Genpei War, demonstrating the growing samurai influence at the imperial court.

EA-JP-054.name: Hōjō Tokiyori and the Mongols
EA-JP-054.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-054.description: Regent Hōjō Tokiyori (r. 1246-1256) strengthened Kamakura's defenses and prepared for the Mongol invasions. His administration balanced samurai, court, and religious interests, a model of medieval Japanese governance.

CA-ST-048.name: Khubilai's Naval Defeats
CA-ST-048.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-048.description: Beyond the failed Japanese invasions, Kublai Khan's fleets also failed against Java, Vietnam, and Burma. These defeats limited Mongol reach into maritime Southeast Asia, allowing those regions to remain independent.

CA-ST-049.name: Mongol Influence on Indian Ocean Trade
CA-ST-049.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-049.description: Mongol peace enabled Indian Ocean trade linking China, India, Persia, and East Africa. Chinese junks, Arab dhows, and Indian vessels carried porcelain, textiles, spices, and precious metals along monsoon routes.

EA-JP-055.name: Onin War (1467-1477)
EA-JP-055.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-055.description: The Onin War, fought between the Yamana and Hosokawa clans in Kyoto, devastated the capital and began the Sengoku (Warring States) period. The Ashikaga shogunate never recovered, and provincial daimyō became independent.

EA-JP-056.name: Rise of the Daimyō
EA-JP-056.domain: East Asia - Unit 5: Late Medieval Empires - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-056.description: After the Onin War, provincial lords (daimyō) consolidated power in their domains, building castles, raising armies, and competing for territory. The daimyō's conflicts defined the Sengoku period.

EA-JP-057.name: Three Unifiers of Japan
EA-JP-057.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-057.description: The proverb "the bird that does not sing, kill it (Oda), make it sing (Hideyoshi), wait for it to sing (Ieyasu)" captures the personalities of the three men who unified Japan: aggressive, clever, and patient.

EA-JP-058.name: Oda Nobunaga (1534-1582)
EA-JP-058.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-058.description: Oda Nobunaga was aggressive and forceful, using violence and new weapons (including European guns acquired from Portuguese traders) to unify Japan quickly. He conquered Kyoto in 1568 and overthrew the last Ashikaga shogun in 1573.

EA-JP-059.name: Battle of Okehazama (1560)
EA-JP-059.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-059.description: Oda Nobunaga's decisive victory over Imagawa Yoshimoto in a sudden rainstorm raid demonstrated his tactical brilliance and willingness to take risks. It launched Oda's unification campaigns from his home base of Owari.

EA-JP-060.name: European Matchlocks in Japan
EA-JP-060.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-060.description: Portuguese traders introduced matchlock firearms (tanegashima) to Japan in 1543, transforming Japanese warfare. Oda Nobunaga deployed massed arquebusiers to devastating effect, ending the era of mounted samurai dominance.

EA-JP-061.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598)
EA-JP-061.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-061.description: Born a commoner, Toyotomi Hideyoshi started as Oda Nobunaga's sandal-bearer. He took control after Oda's death in 1582, became regent to the Emperor, and reunified nearly all of Japan by 1592 through strategy and social control.

EA-JP-062.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Korean Invasions
EA-JP-062.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-062.description: Hideyoshi invaded Korea twice (1592-1593 and 1597-1598) with over 150,000 troops, capturing Seoul and Pyongyang. Korean naval hero Yi Sun-sin and Ming Chinese intervention eventually forced Japanese withdrawal.

EA-JP-063.name: Yi Sun-sin and the Turtle Ships
EA-JP-063.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-063.description: Korean Admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545-1598) defeated the Japanese navy during Hideyoshi's invasions with innovative turtle ships (geobukseon) covered in iron spikes, sustaining a remarkable string of naval victories despite limited resources.

EA-JP-064.name: Sword Hunt (1588)
EA-JP-064.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-064.description: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's "Sword Hunt" (katanagari) separated peasants from weapons, confiscating arms from farmers to prevent rebellion. The decree consolidated military power in the samurai class and redirected agriculture to peaceful pursuits.

EA-JP-065.name: Toyotomi's Taiko Reforms
EA-JP-065.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-065.description: As kampaku (regent, often called "Taiko"), Hideyoshi implemented land surveys (Taikō kenchi), a nationwide cadastral mapping that standardized rice yields and stabilized tax assessment across unified Japan.

EA-JP-066.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616)
EA-JP-066.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-066.description: Tokugawa Ieyasu was patient and calm, waiting for the right moment to seize power. He founded the Tokugawa Shogunate after winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, ruling Japan until 1868 and bringing 250+ years of peace.

EA-JP-067.name: Battle of Sekigahara (1600)
EA-JP-067.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-067.description: The decisive battle in which Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the Toyotomi loyalists, establishing Tokugawa rule. Often compared to other "decisive battles" in world history, it ended the Sengoku period and began Edo Japan.

EA-JP-068.name: Siege of Osaka Castle (1614-1615)
EA-JP-068.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-068.description: The Toyotomi clan's last resistance against Tokugawa Ieyasu. After the Toyotomi defeat, the entire family was destroyed, ending the last major threat to Tokugawa authority and securing the shogunate's 250-year rule.

EA-JP-069.name: Tokugawa Shogunate Founding (1603)
EA-JP-069.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-069.description: In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu received the title of shogun from the emperor, formally establishing the Tokugawa Shogunate in Edo (modern Tokyo). The shogunate would rule Japan for 265 years, the longest in Japanese history.

EA-JP-070.name: Edo Period Social Hierarchy
EA-JP-070.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-070.description: Edo society was rigidly hierarchical: samurai at top, then farmers, artisans, and merchants. The system (shi-nō-kō-shō) was justified by Neo-Confucian philosophy and enforced by sumptuary laws limiting dress and behavior by class.

EA-JP-071.name: Sakoku (Closed Country) Policy
EA-JP-071.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-071.description: From 1633-1639, the Tokugawa Shogunate issued sakoku edicts restricting Japanese contact with foreigners. Dutch and Chinese traders were confined to Dejima island in Nagasaki, and Japanese were forbidden to travel abroad.

EA-JP-072.name: Dejima and Dutch Trading Post
EA-JP-072.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-072.description: Dejima, a small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor, was Japan's only window to Europe during sakoku. Dutch traders brought scientific knowledge (Rangaku, "Dutch learning") and exotic goods, while Japanese scholars learned Western medicine and astronomy.

EA-JP-073.name: Christianity Ban and Martyrdom
EA-JP-073.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-073.description: The Tokugawa Shogunate banned Christianity, viewing it as a cover for European colonization. Christians were forced to renounce their faith (fumie, trampling on Christian images) or face torture and execution. Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan canonized.

EA-JP-074.name: Commodore Perry and Gunboat Diplomacy
EA-JP-074.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-074.description: In 1853, U.S. Commodore Matthew Perry's "Black Ships" arrived in Uraga Harbor demanding Japan open to trade. The shogunate signed the Convention of Kanagawa (1854), ending Japan's 220-year sakoku isolation.

EA-JP-075.name: Treaty of Kanagawa (1854)
EA-JP-075.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-075.description: The first treaty between Japan and the United States, signed under Perry's pressure. It opened two ports to American ships, established a permanent American consulate, and set a precedent for the unequal treaties that followed.

EA-JP-076.name: Christian Persecution in Japan
EA-JP-076.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-076.description: Tokugawa authorities suspected Christians of being foreign agents. The Shimabara Rebellion (1637-1638), led by Christian peasants, was crushed, ending the era of Christian military resistance. Underground Kakure Kirishitan survived in secret.

EA-JP-077.name: Tokugawa Confucianism
EA-JP-077.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-077.description: The Tokugawa Shogunate adopted Neo-Confucianism (especially Zhu Xi's school) as the official ideology, with the Hayashi clan as hereditary Confucian advisors. The philosophy supported the rigid social hierarchy of the period.

EA-JP-078.name: Floating World (Ukiyo) Culture
EA-JP-078.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-078.description: Edo period urban culture celebrated the "floating world" of pleasure quarters, kabuki theater, and ukiyo-e woodblock prints. Writers like Ihara Saikaku and artists like Hokusai and Hiroshige created the distinctive popular art of the era.

EA-JP-079.name: Ukiyo-e Woodblock Prints
EA-JP-079.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-079.description: Ukiyo-e prints depicted kabuki actors, courtesans, landscapes, and folk tales. The collaborative production (artist, carver, printer, publisher) made art widely affordable. Hokusai's "Great Wave" and Hiroshige's "Fifty-Three Stations" became global icons.

EA-JP-080.name: Kabuki Theater
EA-JP-080.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-080.description: Kabuki, developed in the early 17th century by Izumo no Okuni, blended drama, dance, and music. All roles were played by men (the onnagata tradition). The Tokugawa licensed theaters, making them centers of urban entertainment.

EA-JP-081.name: Hokusai and Hiroshige
EA-JP-081.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-081.description: Katsushika Hokusai (1760-1849) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797-1858) were the last great masters of ukiyo-e. Their landscape prints, especially Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, deeply influenced Western Impressionists (Van Gogh, Monet).

EA-JP-082.name: Matsuo Basho and Haiku
EA-JP-082.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-082.description: Matsuo Basho (1644-1694) perfected the haiku form and elevated it to high art. His travel journals like Oku no Hosomichi (Narrow Road to the Deep North) defined the haiku aesthetic of nature, transience, and emotional depth.

EA-JP-083.name: Tokugawa Isolation Effects
EA-JP-083.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-083.description: Sakoku preserved Japanese culture and stability for two centuries but also prevented technological and intellectual exchange. By 1853, Japan lagged behind Western military technology, motivating the rapid Meiji modernization after Perry's arrival.

EA-CH-109.name: Qing Dynasty (1644-1912)
EA-CH-109.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-109.description: Founded by the Manchu Aisin Gioro clan, the Qing Dynasty was the last imperial dynasty of China. It expanded China to its greatest extent, governed a quarter of the world's population, and fell in the 1911 Xinhai Revolution.

EA-CH-110.name: Qing Conquest of China
EA-CH-110.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-110.description: The Manchus under Hong Taiji completed the conquest of Ming China in 1644, exploiting peasant rebel Li Zicheng's brief regime. They proclaimed the Qing Dynasty and gradually extended control over all of China by 1683.

EA-CH-111.name: Kangxi Emperor (r. 1661-1722)
EA-CH-111.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-111.description: The Kangxi Emperor presided over the Qing golden age, defeating the Three Feudatories (1681), reclaiming Taiwan, signing the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia (1689), and patronizing arts, sciences, and Confucian learning.

EA-CH-112.name: Qianlong Emperor (r. 1735-1796)
EA-CH-112.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-112.description: The Qianlong Emperor expanded Qing China to its greatest territorial extent, including Xinjiang, Mongolia, and Tibet. His "Ten Great Campaigns" consolidated frontier regions. He abdicated in 1796 but retained power until his death in 1799.

EA-CH-113.name: Qing Eight Banners System
EA-CH-113.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-113.description: The Manchu military-administrative Eight Banners system organized all Manchu households and absorbed Mongol and Chinese "banner" members. The banners provided cavalry forces but became hereditary, weakening military effectiveness over time.

EA-CH-114.name: Qing Banner and Green Standard
EA-CH-114.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-114.description: The Qing combined the Manchu Eight Banners (elite forces) with the larger Green Standard Army (Han Chinese infantry) for military operations. Banner forces, especially Manchu "Plain Banners," retained privileges over time.

EA-CH-115.name: Qing Population Growth
EA-CH-115.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-115.description: The Qing period saw China's population grow from 150 million to over 400 million, supported by New World crops and political stability. This unprecedented growth strained land resources, leading to internal migrations and environmental pressure.

EA-CH-116.name: Qing Self-Strengthening Movement
EA-CH-116.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-116.description: After defeats in the Opium Wars, some Qing officials led a Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-1895) to modernize military and industry while preserving Confucian tradition. Limited success; the movement ended with Japan's victory in the Sino-Japanese War.

EA-CH-117.name: Qing Imperial Decline
EA-CH-117.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-117.description: The late Qing faced the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864, 20+ million dead), the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901), the Opium Wars (1839-1842, 1856-1860), and territorial losses to Russia, Japan, and European powers. The dynasty fell in 1911.

SA-IN-025.name: Mughal Religious Policy Variations
SA-IN-025.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-025.description: Mughal religious policy varied by ruler: Akbar's tolerance, Jahangir's occasional persecution, Shah Jahan's temple destruction, and Aurangzeb's reimposition of the jizya tax. These shifts shaped Hindu-Muslim relations and Mughal legitimacy.

SA-IN-026.name: Aurangzeb's Deccan Campaigns
SA-IN-026.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-026.description: Aurangzeb spent the last decades of his reign conquering the Deccan sultanates (Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687), expanding the empire to its greatest territorial extent but exhausting finances and military resources.

SA-IN-027.name: Mughal Decline After Aurangzeb
SA-IN-027.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-027.description: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the Mughal Empire fragmented under weak successors and regional powers: the Marathas, the Nawabs of Bengal and Awadh, the Nizam of Hyderabad, and the Sikhs under Ranjit Singh.

SA-IN-028.name: Persian Invasion of Delhi (1739)
SA-IN-028.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-028.description: Nadir Shah of Persia invaded the Mughal Empire in 1739, defeating Emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal and sacking Delhi, including the famous Peacock Throne. The invasion exposed Mughal military weakness and accelerated decline.

SA-IN-029.name: Maratha Confederacy Peak
SA-IN-029.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-029.description: Under Baji Rao I and the Peshwas, the Maratha Confederacy became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century, controlling much of the Deccan and central India, and projecting power into the Gangetic plain.

SA-IN-030.name: European Trading Posts in India
SA-IN-030.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-030.description: The Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British all established trading posts in India from the 16th century. The British East India Company gradually gained political control, exploiting the post-Aurangzeb fragmentation.

CA-ST-050.name: Manchu-Mongol Relations
CA-ST-050.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-050.description: The Qing Manchus, descendants of the Jurchen, cultivated alliances with Mongol tribes through marriages and the Eight Banners. Qing emperors held summer hunts at Chengde to receive Mongol nobles, maintaining steppe ties.

CA-ST-051.name: Russian Expansion into Central Asia
CA-ST-051.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-051.description: From the 16th to 19th centuries, the Russian Empire expanded across Siberia and Central Asia, reaching the Pacific Ocean. Conflicts with the Qing (Amur, Yaksa) and khanates (Bukhara, Khiva, Kokand) reshaped the steppe.

CA-ST-052.name: Nader Shah and Persian Revival
CA-ST-052.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-052.description: Nader Shah (r. 1736-1747), a Turco-Persian warlord, briefly revived Persian power, defeating the Ottomans, invading Mughal India (1739), and projecting influence into Central Asia before his assassination.

EA-KR-015.name: Joseon Korea under Manchu Influence
EA-KR-015.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-015.description: The Joseon Dynasty refused to recognize the Qing initially but was forced to after the Qing invasions of 1627 and 1636 (the Manchu invasions of Korea). Korea became a Qing tributary state while maintaining its Confucian identity.

EA-KR-016.name: Yi Hwang and Yi I (Joseon Confucianism)
EA-KR-016.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-016.description: Yi Hwang (Toegye, 1501-1570) and Yi I (Yulgok, 1536-1584) were the two great Joseon Neo-Confucian philosophers, debating the nature of principle (li) and material force (gi). Their thought shaped Korean scholarship for centuries.

EA-KR-017.name: Hangul Creation (1443-1446)
EA-KR-017.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-017.description: King Sejong the Great commissioned the creation of Hangul, a phonetic alphabet for Korean, in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446. Hangul's scientific design and accessibility made Korea one of the most literate societies in the world.

EA-KR-018.name: Sejong the Great (r. 1418-1450)
EA-KR-018.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-KR civilization
EA-KR-018.description: King Sejong's reign saw the creation of Hangul, astronomical instruments, scientific advances, and the publication of agricultural and medical manuals. He is considered the greatest of all Joseon kings.

CA-ST-053.name: Late Manchu Imperial Expansion
CA-ST-053.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-053.description: Under Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong, the Qing Empire reached its greatest extent: 14.7 million km², including Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang, Taiwan, and Outer Manchuria. The Ten Great Campaigns (1750s-1790s) were the apex of this expansion.

EA-CH-118.name: Qing and Tributary System
EA-CH-118.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-118.description: The Qing maintained the traditional Chinese tribute system, receiving envoys from Korea, Vietnam, Burma, Siam, Ryukyu, and others. The system blended symbolic hierarchy with practical trade and diplomatic relations.

CA-ST-054.name: Qing-Manchu Bilingualism
CA-ST-054.domain: East Asia - Unit 6: Edo Japan and Pre-Modern Asia - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-054.description: Qing emperors were bilingual in Manchu and Chinese, with edicts produced in both languages. The Manchu language preserved as a marker of imperial identity even as most Manchus became culturally sinicized over time.

EA-JP-100.name: Opening of Japan to Western Trade
EA-JP-100.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-100.description: In 1853, U.S. Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Uraga Harbor with a fleet of "Black Ships," demanding Japan open to trade. The Tokugawa Shogunate signed the Convention of Kanagawa in 1854, ending 220 years of sakoku isolation.

EA-JP-101.name: Commodore Matthew Perry
EA-JP-101.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-101.description: Matthew Calbraith Perry (1794-1858) was a U.S. Navy Commodore who commanded the East India Squadron. His 1853 expedition to Japan with four warships opened the country to American trade, ending two centuries of Japanese isolation.

EA-JP-102.name: Black Ships (Kurofune)
EA-JP-102.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-102.description: Perry's fleet of four warships, painted black with advanced steam engines and modern guns, arrived in Japan in 1853. Their overwhelming technological superiority over Japanese defenses convinced the shogunate to negotiate.

EA-JP-103.name: Westward Expansion and Manifest Destiny
EA-JP-103.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-103.description: The U.S. drive to open Japan was fueled by Manifest Destiny, the belief that Americans had a right and duty to spread their land, culture, and government. By 1853, the U.S. sought Pacific trading posts and coaling stations.

EA-JP-104.name: Matthew Perry and the Tokugawa Shogun
EA-JP-104.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-104.description: Perry's 1854 meeting with Tokugawa officials led to the Convention of Kanagawa, despite no actual violence. The treaty opened ports and established a U.S. consul, forcing Japan to engage with Western powers.

EA-JP-105.name: Sakoku Policy Repeal
EA-JP-105.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-105.description: The 1854 Convention of Kanagawa officially ended Japan's sakoku (closed country) policy that had isolated Japan for 220 years under the Tokugawa Shogunate. Japan would soon sign similar unequal treaties with European powers.

EA-JP-106.name: Convention of Kanagawa (1854)
EA-JP-106.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-106.description: The first treaty between the United States and Japan, signed under Perry's threat. It opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships, provided for a U.S. consul, ensured humane treatment of shipwrecked sailors, and began Japan's modernization.

EA-JP-107.name: Dejima Dutch Trading Post
EA-JP-107.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-107.description: During sakoku, the Dutch East India Company was confined to Dejima, a small artificial island in Nagasaki Harbor. Dutch traders were Japan's only window to Europe, bringing scientific knowledge (Rangaku, "Dutch learning").

EA-JP-108.name: Edo Roundtable Debate
EA-JP-108.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-108.description: Students examine sources representing different perspectives on Japan's opening, including the Tokugawa Shogun, samurai commander, daimyo, merchant, Christian convert, peasant farmer, young samurai, Dutch trader, American naval officer, Qing trade official, and Zen Buddhist monk.

EA-JP-109.name: Tokugawa Shogun Perspective on Opening
EA-JP-109.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-109.description: The Tokugawa Shogun was responsible for maintaining order in Japan. Sources supporting a closed-country stance argued sakoku had brought peace and stability during the Edo Period by restricting foreign influence and Christianity.

EA-JP-110.name: Christian Convert Perspective on Opening
EA-JP-110.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-110.description: Japanese Christians had been persecuted for centuries under the Tokugawa ban on Christianity, with martyrs executed and believers forced to renounce their faith. They had strong reasons to favor opening for religious freedom.

EA-JP-111.name: American Naval Officer Perspective on Opening
EA-JP-111.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-111.description: U.S. naval officers like Perry saw opening Japan as part of American commercial and strategic interests, seeking coaling stations for steamships and new markets for American goods in Asia.

EA-JP-112.name: Japanese Steam and Steamship Technology Gap
EA-JP-112.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-112.description: Perry's "Black Ships" demonstrated Western steam-powered iron warships with advanced gunpowder weapons. The visual contrast with Japanese sailing ships shocked Japan and motivated rapid Meiji-era modernization.

EA-JP-113.name: Sino-American Trade Imbalance
EA-JP-113.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-113.description: European trade with Qing China was restricted to Guangzhou under the Canton System. Britain purchased tea, silk, and porcelain, while China accumulated silver and cotton, creating a heavy trade imbalance favoring China.

EA-JP-114.name: Macartney Embassy (1793)
EA-JP-114.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-114.description: In 1793, British envoy George Macartney was sent to China to open trade but was rejected by the Qianlong Emperor. The failed embassy intensified European interest in finding new ways to engage with China.

EA-CH-141.name: Canton System (1757)
EA-CH-141.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-141.description: Established by the Qianlong Emperor in 1757, the Canton System restricted all European trade to Guangzhou (Canton). European merchants were required to stay within the Thirteen Factories commercial district, with no access to inland China.

EA-CH-142.name: Qianlong Emperor and Trade Restrictions
EA-CH-142.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-142.description: The Qianlong Emperor established the Canton System in 1757 to limit European contact and protect Chinese society from foreign influence. He famously told King George III that China had no need for British goods.

EA-CH-143.name: Thirteen Factories
EA-CH-143.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-143.description: The Thirteen Factories was a commercial district in Guangzhou where European merchants were required to live and conduct trade. The system regulated contact between Chinese and foreign traders under strict Qing supervision.

EA-CH-144.name: Guangzhou Trade Monopoly
EA-CH-144.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-144.description: The Cohong system licensed a small number of Chinese merchant guilds to handle all foreign trade in Guangzhou. The Hoppo (imperial customs superintendent) regulated prices and collected duties on all transactions.

EA-CH-145.name: Mercantilist Canton System
EA-CH-145.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-145.description: The Canton System reflected Qing mercantilist policy: export as much as possible, import as little as possible. The goal was to accumulate silver while limiting European presence and influence in China.

SA-IN-060.name: Industrial Revolution in Britain
SA-IN-060.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-060.description: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 18th century, transforming Britain from an agricultural to an industrial society. Britain's coal, capital, colonies, and political stability gave it unique advantages for industrialization.

SA-IN-061.name: Why Industrialization Began in Britain
SA-IN-061.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-061.description: Britain's industrialization started because of large, easy-to-reach coal deposits; wood shortages; frequent mine flooding (sparking steam engine innovation); a wealthy ruling class willing to invest; little government involvement; and a strong navy to protect commerce.

SA-IN-062.name: Steam Engine Innovation
SA-IN-062.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-062.description: The steam engine, pioneered by Thomas Newcomen and improved by James Watt, solved the problem of flooding in British coal mines. It became the driving force of the Industrial Revolution, powering factories, mines, and eventually steamships and railroads.

SA-IN-063.name: British Coal and Industrial Resources
SA-IN-063.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-063.description: Britain had large, easily accessible coal deposits located close to rivers for transport. This abundant fuel source was essential for the steam engines that powered industrial machinery.

SA-IN-064.name: Atlantic Slave Trade and British Capital
SA-IN-064.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-064.description: Profits from the transatlantic slave trade gave Britain capital to invest in industrialization. British colonies in the Americas, Africa, and India provided land, natural resources, labor, and markets for factory-made goods.

SA-IN-065.name: Why Industrialization Did Not Start in China
SA-IN-065.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-CH civilization
SA-IN-065.description: China did not industrialize first because its coal was far from business centers and rivers; it had a large cheap labor force reducing machine incentives; cultural ideals valued stability over change; and dry coal mines didn't need pumping machines.

SA-IN-066.name: East India Company and India
SA-IN-066.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-066.description: The British East India Company (EIC), chartered in 1600, gradually took control of India. The 1757 Battle of Plassey began 100 years of BEIC colonial rule. India was not directly ruled by the British government until 1858.

SA-IN-067.name: Battle of Plassey (1757)
SA-IN-067.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-067.description: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 was fought between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal. Robert Clive's victory with a small force of 3,000 (against 50,000) began British dominance of India.

SA-IN-068.name: BEIC Bengal Cotton
SA-IN-068.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-068.description: Bengali farmers sent raw cotton to Britain, where factories produced cheap textiles that were sold back to India. The British destroyed Bengali textile industries through tariffs, ensuring a captive market for British goods.

SA-IN-069.name: Bengal as Captive Market
SA-IN-069.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-069.description: Bengal was one of the richest and most populated territories in the world. After the EIC takeover, Indians who wanted cotton textiles had to buy them from Britain, creating a guaranteed market for British industrial output.

SA-IN-070.name: Mughal Empire Decline
SA-IN-070.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-070.description: The Mughal Empire was one of the most powerful states in the world in the 17th-18th centuries, but it did not officially end until 1858. Between 1757 (Plassey) and 1858, India was under BEIC colonial rule, with the British crown gradually assuming direct control.

SA-IN-071.name: British East India Company Monopoly
SA-IN-071.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - SA-IN civilization
SA-IN-071.description: The EIC had a monopoly on British trade with India and China. It governed large parts of India with its own private army, sometimes more powerful than Britain's military, before the British government took over after the 1857 Sepoy Mutiny.

SA-CH-146.name: Opium and the Poppy
SA-CH-146.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
SA-CH-146.description: Opium is a drug made from the latex of the poppy flower, causing sleepiness, lack of fear, peaceful feelings, and hallucinations. Highly addictive, with severe withdrawal including anxiety, depression, pain, and sometimes death.

EA-CH-147.name: British Opium Trade with China
EA-CH-147.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-147.description: After taking Bengal, the EIC shifted Indian agriculture from cotton to opium production. Opium grown in India was sold around the world, especially to China, as a highly profitable (and addictive) commodity.

EA-CH-148.name: Qianlong Emperor Bans Opium (1796)
EA-CH-148.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-148.description: In 1796, the Qianlong Emperor banned the import of opium to China, recognizing its devastating effects on the population. Despite the ban, the EIC continued to smuggle opium through Chinese merchants.

EA-CH-149.name: Illegal Opium Trade
EA-CH-149.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-149.description: The EIC illegally sold opium to Chinese merchants, who paid in silver. This reversed the favorable Qing trade balance, drained Chinese silver reserves, and caused widespread addiction across Chinese society.

EA-CH-150.name: Lin Zexu Anti-Opium Campaign
EA-CH-150.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-150.description: Lin Zexu, the Chinese governor of southern provinces, led a vigorous anti-opium campaign from 1837-1840. In 1839, he ordered foreign merchants to surrender their opium stocks and oversaw the destruction of 1,200 tons at Humen.

EA-CH-151.name: Humen Opium Destruction (1839)
EA-CH-151.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-151.description: In June 1839, Lin Zexu ordered the destruction of 1,200 tons of confiscated British opium at Humen. Some was destroyed in international waters in violation of standard practice. The British demanded compensation China deemed excessive.

EA-CH-152.name: Lin Zexu Letter to Queen Victoria
EA-CH-152.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-152.description: In 1839, Lin Zexu wrote to Queen Victoria asking why Britain would not stop the opium trade: "Suppose there were people from another country who carried opium for sale to England and seduced your people into buying and smoking it..."

EA-CH-153.name: First Opium War (1839-1842)
EA-CH-153.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-153.description: The First Opium War lasted three years (1839-1842). British forces (~20,000) decisively defeated Qing forces (~220,000, but only 100,000 in battle). British casualties were 70 killed; Qing casualties were ~3,100.

EA-CH-154.name: HMS Nemesis and Modern Naval Power
EA-CH-154.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-154.description: The HMS Nemesis, an iron steam ship operated by the EIC, destroyed Chinese war junks in 1841 using modern steam propulsion. The contrast with wooden Chinese ships demonstrated the military technology gap.

EA-CH-155.name: Treaty of Nanjing (1842)
EA-CH-155.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-155.description: Signed in 1842 after the First Opium War, the Treaty of Nanjing was the first "unequal treaty" imposed on China. It established treaty ports, granted extraterritoriality to British citizens, and ceded Hong Kong to Britain.

EA-CH-156.name: Unequal Treaties System
EA-CH-156.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-156.description: The Qing signed more unequal treaties with the United States, France, and other powers. Later, Japan, Korea, and Thailand entered similar treaties. These established the "century of humiliation" framework in Chinese history.

EA-CH-157.name: Treaty Ports
EA-CH-157.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-157.description: Treaty ports were cities opened to foreign trade by unequal treaties. The Treaty of Nanjing opened Guangzhou, Xiamen, Ningbo, Fuzhou, and Shanghai. These ports became centers of foreign economic influence and cultural exchange.

EA-CH-158.name: Extraterritoriality
EA-CH-158.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-158.description: Extraterritoriality meant that if a foreigner committed a crime in a Chinese treaty port, they were tried by their own country's courts, not Chinese courts. This undermined Chinese sovereignty and created foreign "extraterritorial" enclaves.

EA-CH-159.name: Hong Kong Ceded to Britain
EA-CH-159.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-159.description: Hong Kong island was ceded to Britain as a colony under the Treaty of Nanjing (1842). It remained a British possession until its 1997 handover to China, symbolizing the "century of humiliation."

EA-CH-160.name: Second Opium War (1856-1860)
EA-CH-160.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-160.description: The Second Opium War (Arrow War) was fought between the Qing and Britain, France, the United States (small force), and Russia (no soldiers). It resulted in new treaties, more treaty ports, legalization of opium, and destruction of Beijing's Yuanmingyuan.

EA-CH-161.name: Yuanmingyuan Destruction (1860)
EA-CH-161.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-161.description: During the Second Opium War, Anglo-French forces looted and burned the Yuanmingyuan (Old Summer Palace) in Beijing. The destruction symbolized the depths of Qing humiliation and remained a major source of Chinese resentment toward Western powers.

EA-CH-162.name: Opium Trade Legalization
EA-CH-162.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-162.description: A result of the Second Opium War was the legalization of the opium trade in China. This further devastated Chinese society, with addiction spreading across classes and regions, draining silver and labor from the economy.

EA-CH-163.name: Century of Humiliation
EA-CH-163.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-163.description: The "Century of Humiliation" (1839-1949) refers to the period from the First Opium War to the Communist victory. The term captures the cumulative effects of unequal treaties, territorial losses, and foreign intervention in Chinese affairs.

EA-CH-164.name: Imperialism Definition
EA-CH-164.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-164.description: Imperialism occurs when a powerful country takes control over a weaker country or area economically, politically, or militarily. Imperialism can occur from afar (e.g., through economic leverage), distinct from colonization which requires physical settlement.

EA-JP-115.name: Satsuma and Choshu Domains
EA-JP-115.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-115.description: The Satsuma domain (southern Kyushu) and Choshu domain (western Honshu) were the most powerful "outside" domains that led the Meiji Restoration. Their samurai recognized that the Tokugawa Shogunate was too weak to resist Western imperialism.

EA-JP-116.name: Boshin War Origins
EA-JP-116.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-116.description: The Boshin War (1868-1869) was fought between imperial forces and the Tokugawa Shogunate. It began when Satsuma-Choshu forces seized Kyoto and declared the restoration of imperial rule, prompting loyalist domains to support the shogun.

EA-JP-117.name: Satsuma Rebellion (1877)
EA-JP-117.domain: East Asia - Unit 7: Industrialization and Imperialism - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-117.description: Led by Saigo Takamori, the Satsuma Rebellion was the last major samurai uprising against the Meiji government. The modern conscript army decisively defeated the rebels, ending armed resistance to modernization.

EA-JP-118.name: Meiji Restoration (1868)
EA-JP-118.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-118.description: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 restored practical power to the Japanese Emperor, ending 700 years of samurai-dominated shogunate rule. Young Emperor Meiji and reformist samurai from Satsuma and Choshu domains launched rapid modernization.

EA-JP-119.name: Civil War in Japan (Boshin War)
EA-JP-119.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-119.description: The Boshin War (1868-1869) was the brief civil war fought between imperial forces and the Tokugawa Shogunate. The war consolidated Meiji power and led to the abolition of the 700-year-old shogunate system.

EA-JP-120.name: Meiji Era 45 Years
EA-JP-120.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-120.description: The 45 years of the Emperor Meiji's reign (1868-1912) is known as the Meiji Era or Meiji Restoration, a period of rapid Westernization, industrialization, and imperial expansion that transformed Japan from a feudal society into a modern nation-state.

EA-JP-121.name: Tokyo as New Capital
EA-JP-121.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-121.description: The Meiji government moved the imperial capital from Kyoto to Tokyo (formerly the samurai capital of Edo). The name change ("Eastern Capital") symbolized the new era's break with feudal traditions.

EA-JP-122.name: Meiji Restoration Definitions
EA-JP-122.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-122.description: The Meiji Restoration involved two interrelated processes: the political restoration of imperial rule (overthrowing the Tokugawa Shogunate) and the cultural/technological restoration of Japan as a great power through Western-style modernization.

EA-JP-123.name: Nationalism and Meiji Restoration
EA-JP-123.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-123.description: The Meiji Restoration was driven by rising Japanese nationalism and the slogan "Sonno Joi" (Revere the Emperor, Expel the Barbarians). Ironically, the "expel the barbarians" goal was replaced by "learn from the barbarians" (Western models).

EA-JP-124.name: Fukuzawa Yukichi and "Datsu-A Ron"
EA-JP-124.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-124.description: Fukuzawa Yukichi (1835-1901), the most influential Meiji intellectual, authored "Departure from Asia" (Datsu-A Ron, 1885), arguing Japan must abandon Asian traditions and join the civilized Western nations. His writings shaped Meiji nationalism.

EA-JP-125.name: 1889 Meiji Constitution
EA-JP-125.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-125.description: The 1889 Meiji Constitution, modeled on the Prussian Constitution, was "given" to the people by the emperor. Only he (or his advisers) could change it, establishing a constitutional monarchy with a bicameral Diet.

EA-JP-126.name: Constitutional Government Modeled on Germany
EA-JP-126.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-126.description: The Meiji Constitution created a constitutional government modeled after the German system, with strong executive power centered in the emperor. This gave Japan a modern constitutional form while preserving imperial sovereignty.

EA-JP-127.name: Article 1: Imperial Lineage
EA-JP-127.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-127.description: Chapter I, Article 1 of the Meiji Constitution states: "The Empire of Japan shall be reigned over and governed by a line of Emperors unbroken for ages eternal." This established the emperor as the sovereign of Japan.

EA-JP-128.name: Article 3: Sacred and Inviolable Emperor
EA-JP-128.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-128.description: Article 3 of the Meiji Constitution declared: "The Emperor is sacred and inviolable." This sacred status was later renounced by Emperor Hirohito in the 1946 Humanity Declaration after Japan's WWII defeat.

EA-JP-129.name: Article 4: Sovereign Rights
EA-JP-129.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-129.description: Article 4 of the Meiji Constitution states: "The Emperor is the head of the Empire, combining in Himself the rights of sovereignty, and exercises them, according to the provisions of the present Constitution."

EA-JP-130.name: Imperial Diet and Emperor's Powers
EA-JP-130.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-130.description: Article 7 of the Meiji Constitution states: "The Emperor convokes the Imperial Diet, opens, closes, and prorogues it, and dissolves the House of Representatives." The Diet was consultative; the emperor held sovereign power.

EA-JP-131.name: Universal Public Education (1872)
EA-JP-131.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-131.description: The 1872 Fundamental Code of Education established a universal public education system where all children were allowed to go to school for free. This dismantled the previous system where learning was the prerogative of samurai and courtiers.

EA-JP-132.name: Education for All Classes
EA-JP-132.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-132.description: After the Meiji Restoration, farmers, artisans, and merchants gained access to education previously reserved for samurai. Universal public education created a literate citizenry capable of supporting Japan's industrial modernization.

EA-JP-133.name: Ministry of Education (Japan)
EA-JP-133.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-133.description: The Ministry of Education of Japan (established 1871) implemented the universal education system. By 1890, the school system was well-established, with mandatory attendance for children, supporting Japan's rapid modernization.

EA-JP-134.name: Meiji Modernization Pillars
EA-JP-134.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-134.description: Meiji modernization rested on four pillars: (1) abolition of feudal domains, (2) establishment of a conscript army, (3) building of railroads and telegraphs, and (4) adoption of a German-style constitution and Western institutions.

EA-JP-135.name: Iwakura Mission (1871-1873)
EA-JP-135.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-135.description: The Iwakura Mission sent Japanese officials on a nearly two-year world tour to study Western governments, industries, and education systems. Their reports guided Meiji reforms, including adoption of Western legal codes, postal systems, and railways.

EA-JP-136.name: Abolition of Feudal Domains
EA-JP-136.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-136.description: The Meiji government abolished the feudal han (domains) system in 1871, replacing domain lords with centrally-appointed governors. This centralized power in Tokyo, ending the autonomy that had enabled domains like Satsuma and Choshu to challenge the shogunate.

EA-JP-137.name: Meiji Conscript Army
EA-JP-137.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-137.description: The Meiji government established a conscript army in 1873, replacing the samurai monopoly on military service. The new army, modeled on European forces, allowed Japan to raise a modern military capable of defeating China (1895) and Russia (1905).

EA-JP-138.name: Haitōrei: Sword Abolition (1876)
EA-JP-138.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-138.description: The Meiji government's Haitōrei decree banned the wearing of swords by samurai, ending their visible status symbol. Combined with the loss of samurai stipends, this spurred the Satsuma Rebellion (1877), the last major armed samurai resistance.

EA-JP-139.name: Treaty Revision under Meiji
EA-JP-139.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-139.description: The Meiji government made revision of the unequal treaties a major goal, finally achieved in 1894 with the Anglo-Japanese Treaty. The success demonstrated Japan's emergence as a modern nation-state recognized by Western powers.

EA-JP-140.name: First Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895)
EA-JP-140.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-140.description: Japan's victory over Qing China in the First Sino-Japanese War demonstrated the success of Meiji modernization. The Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895) gave Japan Taiwan, the Pescadores, and a large indemnity, marking Japan's emergence as a regional power.

EA-JP-141.name: Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905)
EA-JP-141.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-141.description: Japan's stunning victory over Russia, including the naval Battle of Tsushima (1905), was the first time a non-Western power defeated a European power in modern warfare. It established Japan as a world power.

EA-JP-142.name: Japanese Colonial Empire
EA-JP-142.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-142.description: Following the First Sino-Japanese War, Japan acquired Taiwan (1895), Korea (annexed 1910), and other territories. This built a short-lived colonial empire that would later expand into the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere during WWII.

EA-CH-165.name: Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901)
EA-CH-165.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-165.description: The Boxer Rebellion was an anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in northern China led by the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists. After the Qing initially supported the Boxers, the Eight-Nation Alliance crushed the rebellion, imposing the Boxer Protocol.

EA-CH-166.name: Boxers (Yihequan)
EA-CH-166.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-166.description: The "Boxers" (Yihequan, "Righteous and Harmonious Fists") were a secretive anti-foreign group whose official name was the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists. They saw themselves as defenders of Chinese culture, blaming foreign influence and Christianity for China's problems.

EA-CH-167.name: Boxer Anti-Foreign Sentiment
EA-CH-167.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-167.description: In the late 1800s, several powerful foreign nations forced China to sign unequal treaties following military defeats. Many Chinese felt outsiders were taking over their country, fueling anger at the Qing government for failing to resist foreign encroachment.

EA-CH-168.name: Boxer Loyalty to Chinese Culture
EA-CH-168.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-168.description: The Boxers were very loyal to Chinese culture. They saw themselves as defenders of China, blaming China's growing problems on foreign influence and Christianity. They believed they could restore purity by removing foreign influences.

EA-CH-169.name: Boxer Anti-Christian Violence
EA-CH-169.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-169.description: As support for the Boxer movement spread, its members began carrying out increasingly aggressive actions. Chinese Christians were seen as having abandoned traditional Chinese beliefs, making them targets of violence.

EA-CH-170.name: Boxer Beliefs in Ritual Purity
EA-CH-170.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-170.description: The Boxers believed they could make Chinese society "pure" again by removing foreign influences. They also believed they could resist bullets through ritual practices and martial arts, contributing to their willingness to confront modern firearms.

EA-CH-171.name: Qing Divided Response to Boxers
EA-CH-171.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-171.description: At the beginning of the Boxer uprising, the Qing government was deeply divided and uncertain about how to respond. Some officials supported the Boxers, while others favored suppression. The Empress Dowager Cixi eventually sided with the Boxers.

EA-CH-172.name: Eight-Nation Alliance Intervention
EA-CH-172.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-172.description: In response to the growing violence of the Boxer Rebellion and the Qing government's official support, the Eight-Nation Alliance (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, United States, Italy, Austria-Hungary) sent troops to crush the rebellion.

EA-CH-173.name: Boxer Protocol (1901)
EA-CH-173.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-173.description: The Boxer Protocol ended the Boxer Rebellion with harsh terms for China. It required execution of Qing officials, payment of 450 million taels of silver in indemnities, and the stationing of foreign troops in Beijing, deepening the "century of humiliation."

EA-CH-174.name: Boxer Rebellion Lasting Impact
EA-CH-174.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-174.description: Although the Boxer Rebellion ended in military defeat, it had a lasting impact. Unlike the earlier Self-Strengthening Movement (which preserved tradition), the Boxers demonstrated that cultural resistance alone could not match modern industrial powers.

EA-CH-175.name: Self-Strengthening Movement Failure
EA-CH-175.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-175.description: The Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-1895) attempted to adopt Western technology while preserving Confucian tradition. Its failure, demonstrated by Japan's 1895 victory, showed that selective Westernization was insufficient.

EA-CH-176.name: Foreign Troops in Beijing
EA-CH-176.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-176.description: The Boxer Protocol allowed foreign troops to be stationed in Beijing to protect legation districts. This was a major violation of Chinese sovereignty and a visible symbol of Qing weakness, remaining in place until 1943.

EA-CH-177.name: Qing Government's Boxer Support
EA-CH-177.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-177.description: Empress Dowager Cixi's decision to support the Boxers in 1900 marked a fatal strategic error. The Qing government's open embrace of the movement gave the foreign powers a pretext for their intervention, ensuring the rebellion's military defeat.

CA-ST-060.name: Eight-Nation Alliance Composition
CA-ST-060.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-060.description: The Eight-Nation Alliance that intervened in the Boxer Rebellion included Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the United States, Italy, and Austria-Hungary. Japan sent the largest contingent, gaining prestige as an emerging power.

CA-ST-061.name: Russian Role in Boxer Intervention
CA-ST-061.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-061.description: Russia used the Boxer Rebellion as a pretext to expand its presence in Manchuria. Russian troops occupied key positions in northern China, contributing to later tensions with Japan that erupted in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905).

CA-ST-062.name: Japan's Role in Boxer Intervention
CA-ST-062.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-062.description: Japan, the only Asian power in the Eight-Nation Alliance, sent the largest contingent of troops to suppress the Boxer Rebellion. This demonstrated Japan's emergence as a regional power and earned it respect among Western nations.

EA-CH-178.name: Anti-Christian Violence in China
EA-CH-178.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-178.description: Chinese Christians were seen as people who had given up traditional Chinese beliefs and were allied with foreign powers. The Boxers targeted them with violence, including killings, as part of their campaign to "purify" Chinese society.

EA-CH-179.name: Missionaries in Late Qing China
EA-CH-179.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-179.description: Western Christian missionaries had been active in China since the 16th century, with major expansion in the 19th century after the unequal treaties. They established schools, hospitals, and churches, sometimes providing education to women and lower classes.

EA-CH-180.name: Concessions and Spheres of Influence
EA-CH-180.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-180.description: After the unequal treaties, foreign powers carved China into "spheres of influence": Britain in the Yangtze Valley, Russia in Manchuria, Germany in Shandong, France in the south, and Japan in Fujian. These divisions accelerated later conflicts.

EA-CH-181.name: Open Door Policy (1899-1900)
EA-CH-181.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-181.description: U.S. Secretary of State John Hay's Open Door Policy (1899-1900) sought to preserve China's territorial integrity and prevent any single power from monopolizing trade. The policy was largely rhetorical but shaped U.S.-China relations for decades.

EA-CH-182.name: Boxer Indemnity Scholarship Program
EA-CH-182.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-182.description: A portion of the Boxer Indemnity paid by China was later returned to fund Chinese students studying in the United States. This Boxer Indemnity Scholarship Program trained generations of Chinese leaders, including architect I.M. Pei.

EA-CH-183.name: Aftermath of the Boxer Rebellion
EA-CH-183.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-183.description: The Boxer Rebellion's defeat accelerated Qing decline and stimulated both reform (the late Qing New Policies) and revolution (Sun Yat-sen's movement). It marked the final breakdown of the traditional Confucian order in China.

EA-CH-184.name: Late Qing New Policies (1901-1911)
EA-CH-184.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-184.description: Following the Boxer defeat, the Qing implemented sweeping New Policies: abolition of the civil service exams (1905), creation of a modern school system, provincial assemblies, and a constitutional reform process. These were insufficient to save the dynasty.

EA-CH-185.name: New Army in Late Qing
EA-CH-185.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-185.description: The New Armies (Xinjun) created after the Boxer Rebellion were trained in modern warfare. Ironically, these armies became the foundations of regional warlord power after the 1911 revolution, undermining central authority.

EA-JP-143.name: Japan's Pre-War Imperialism
EA-JP-143.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-143.description: Following the Meiji Restoration, Japan joined the ranks of imperial powers, gaining Taiwan (1895), the Pescadores, Karafuto/Sakhalin, and Korea (1910). Japan's colonial empire was a major cause of pre-WWII Asian tensions.

EA-CH-186.name: Late Qing Reform Attempts
EA-CH-186.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-186.description: After the Boxer defeat, the Qing court attempted reforms including establishing provincial assemblies, modernizing the legal code, and creating modern industries. These reforms were too late and too limited to save the dynasty.

CA-ST-063.name: Russian Far East Expansion
CA-ST-063.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - CA-ST civilization
CA-ST-063.description: Russia's expansion into Manchuria during the Boxer Rebellion included the construction of the Chinese Eastern Railway, giving Russia control over transportation in northeastern China and setting the stage for later conflicts with Japan.

EA-CH-187.name: Chinese Eastern Railway
EA-CH-187.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-CH civilization
EA-CH-187.description: Built by Russia across Manchuria in 1898-1903, the Chinese Eastern Railway connected the Trans-Siberian Railway to Port Arthur and Dalian. It symbolized Russian imperial control of China's northeast, fueling later conflicts with Japan.

EA-JP-144.name: Port Arthur and Liaodong Lease
EA-JP-144.domain: East Asia - Unit 8: Meiji Restoration and Boxer Rebellion - EA-JP civilization
EA-JP-144.description: After the First Sino-Japanese War, Japan gained the Liaodong Peninsula (including Port Arthur) and southern Manchurian railway rights. Russia, France, and Germany forced Japan to return the peninsula, then Russia leased it in 1898.
